entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• In the year after Israel left Egypt, the Lord often communicated his will to the people through Moses, giving them many chances to follow his divine plan. 

• God often revealed himself in the Tent of Meeting; see study note on Exodus 27:21. 

• The wilderness of Sinai was a vast, frightening, and harsh desert (Deuteronomy 1:19). This mostly empty area was where God matured Israel. The challenges of Sinai's harsh living conditions tested Israel's reliance on the Lord throughout the book of Numbers. Sinai reminded later biblical authors of the law and Israel's rebellious spirit (Psalm 106:19; Hebrews 12:25–26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God chose a family leader from each tribe (except the tribe of Levi), to count Israel's men who were old enough to be soldiers.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites got ready to leave for the promised land by listing all troops who could join the conquest. The nation was changing from slavery to becoming a nation.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• those who are twenty years of age or older by their divisions—everyone who can serve in Israel’s army: This registration gathered more information than the earlier census (compare Exodus 38:26). 

• These are the names of the men who are to assist you: Hebrew culture was tribal, centered around clans and families. They easily identified the tribal leaders, who appear again as a group in Numbers 7. 

• Moses and Aaron did not include the tribe of Levi in this registration because it had a special status in Israelite society (see Numbers 1:47–53; Numbers 26:51–62; Deuteronomy 18:5; Deuteronomy 33:8–11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: These tribal leaders proved to be responsible and trustworthy by completing other important tasks.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The count of 603,550 shows the same number of qualified men as mentioned in Exodus 38:26. Exodus 12:37 and Numbers 11:21 give an approximate number of 600,000. 

People have interpreted these numbers in different ways:

• The numbers might show the actual size of this army (see Exodus 1:9–10). 

• The numbers might be symbolic. A later editor might have estimated, or might have misunderstood while translating. 

See also study note on Exodus 12:37.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The second list of tribes lists Gad with Reuben and Simeon. These two tribes camped with Gad while Israel traveled.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribe of Levi did not serve in Israel's army like the other tribes. This part of Numbers explains how the Levites organized to serve in the tabernacle of the Testimony, which was their main duty.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: tabernacle of the Testimony: This was a portable sanctuary. It symbolized the Lord’s presence and showed Israel’s covenant relationship with him.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Levites had the job of setting up, taking down, moving, and guarding the tabernacle. They kept unauthorized people from coming too close or making it unclean. This protected the Israelites from the Lord's judgment.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel organized its camps by tribal groups. This probably addressed social status, water access, and security for the Tent of Meeting. This tent represented the Lord's presence. The Egyptian army from around the same time period used a similar defensive formation to protect holy objects during their battle campaigns.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Each area of the Hebrew camp had family banners, probably flags or streamers (Numbers 1:52). Modern Bedouins also use tribal symbols or battle flags. This shows the continued importance of tribe, clan, and family divisions. 

• The tribes camped around the holy place at a safe distance (compare Joshua 3:4). This respected the distinction between God's holiness and the non-Levitical tribes.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun camped in the most important spot on the east side of the Tent of Meeting. They led when Israel traveled. This largest tribal group had 186,400 people. It could protect the holy tent and its assistants very well.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad camped on the south. They had 151,450 soldiers and marched second in line.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin followed the Tent of Meeting and the Levites.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribes of Dan, Asher, and Naphtali were in the back.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: At first, the Hebrews obeyed God's commands by camping and marching as Moses instructed. Yet, they soon stopped being obedient.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Aaron's family line provided the priests who led Israel's worship. Aaron's four sons were the core of Israel's priesthood. They served in God's presence on behalf of the people. God chose (ordained) them to lead and serve as ministers in the Tent of Meeting. They also acted as guardians of God's covenant with his people.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel's priests and Levites had duties like moving, assembling, protecting, and maintaining the Tent of Meeting. The way God organized the tribes highlighted his concern for these priestly tasks.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The deaths of Nadab and Abihu (see Leviticus 10:1–2) showed the need to protect the holiness of the sanctuary and to strictly obey God's instructions (Numbers 26:61; Leviticus 16:1; 1 Chronicles 24:2; compare Acts 5:1–11; 1 Corinthians 10:6–11; 1 Corinthians 11:29–30). 

• Eleazar and Ithamar: See “Eleazar” Profile.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God chose the Levites to be assistants for the priests, represented by Aaron. They had a number of holy duties in their ministry service. They performed holy tasks to maintain the Tent of Meeting and its items (Numbers 3:7,8; explained more in Numbers 4:1–33).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The sanctuary was set apart for God’s holy use (Numbers 1:51; Numbers 3:38; Numbers 18:7). Only qualified people could approach it (compare Numbers 3:4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• every firstborn Israelite: These belonged to God because God spared them when the Egyptian firstborn sons died (Numbers 3:13; see Exodus 11–12). 

• I have taken the Levites: God chose the Levites to serve as substitutes for the firstborn sons.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• This first phase of a two-part registration of the tribe of Levi summarized each family's special duties. Numbers 4:1–33 describes this in more detail (see Numbers 4:34–49 for the second phase). This count did not relate to military duties, so it included male Levites from the age of one month (Numbers 3:40–41).

• Three family groups descend from the three sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. These clans, often called the Gershonites, Kohathites, and Merarites, later inherited the "cities of refuge" (Joshua 21). They also had various important roles in the Jerusalem temple (2 Chronicles 29:3–17).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Aaron and Moses, sons of Amram, were descendants of Kohath (see Exodus 6:18, Exodus 6:20, Exodus 6:26). They were caretakers of the Most Holy Place and its very holy furnishings (described in Numbers 3–4). The Kohathites were the most respected of the three clans.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: 8,600: Some ancient Greek versions say 8,300. The “six” (Hebrew shsh) in 8,600 could result from misreading a “three” (Hebrew shlsh).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Aaron’s third son, Eleazar, led the Levites as an administrator. He was like an executive secretary, while his father did other tasks. He had "oversight of the entire tabernacle" (Numbers 4:16–20). Eleazar had a key role during Israel’s time in the wilderness. He later became the high priest after his father (see Numbers 16:37–39; Numbers 19:3–6; Numbers 20:25–28; Numbers 26:1–3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The best campsite east of the tabernacle was for Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: 22,000: The numbers for each clan totaled 22,300 (Numbers 3:22, Numbers 3:28, Numbers 3:34). See the study note on 3:28.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
There were 273 more firstborn sons in Israel from the non-Levite tribes than there were Levite males (compare Leviticus 3:39). The Levites acted as substitutes for Israel's firstborn sons (Numbers 3:41; see study note on 3:11–13). The law required a redemption price of five pieces of silver for each extra firstborn son (Numbers 3:46–48; compare Leviticus 27:6). 

It is unclear who paid this cost. This arrangement for special substitutes points to Christ’s role as a substitute. Through his death, Christ paid the redemption price for all humanity (see Mark 10:45; Galatians 3:13; Ephesians 1:7; Hebrews 9:15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses and Aaron communicated God's will about the care and transport of the Tent of Meeting. This was the main duty of the three Levitical families.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• This section continues the discussion from Numbers 3:21–37 about the duties of the three Levite clans. The Levites carried and cared for the Tent of Meeting while traveling and camping. Other tribes always surrounded them to protect them and their valuable cargo (Numbers 2:17). They placed the holy items of God in the center of the tribes. The priests and their Levitical assistants kept these items holy by separating them. 

• God, in his holiness, deserves to have the details of his will given careful attention. The Tent of Meeting and its furnishings were holy. The tribe of Levi had to maintain the difference between holy and common, and between ceremonially clean and unclean. This is why there is so much information about the duties of the three Levite clans.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Out of the 22,000 Levites, only men aged thirty to fifty could serve in the sanctuary (Numbers 3:39). This was because they were most capable at this time of their lives. Numbers 4:34–49 lists 8,580 qualified males. This is the summary of this registration, another "numbering."

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The duties of the Kohathites come first because they handled the most holy objects (see Numbers 3:27–32). This might be because Aaron and the priests came from this clan (1 Chronicles 6:2–3). Their tasks included carrying, setting up, and folding up these holy and very important coverings and furnishings. 

The items entrusted to Kohath's descendants were very valuable. These included: 

• the ark of the Testimony, 

• the table of the Bread of the Presence, 

• the lampstand (Hebrew menorah), 

• the gold incense altar, and 

• the altar for sacrifices. 

Exodus 25–30 first describes these objects. But Numbers shows how the Hebrews used them in daily life. The Kohathites carried these items on poles or in frames. They could not touch them or enter the sanctuary to look at them, or they would die.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Aaron and his sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, had to fully cover the sanctuary and all holy items before the camp could move. Non-Levitical tribes marched in front and behind the Levites, who carried the Tent of Meeting. The colors of the coverings showed the royalty of the objects. 

They were so holy that even the Kohathites, whom God chose to handle them, could not touch the holy items, or they would die. This respect showed the holiness of Israel's Lord. Ignoring these rules was dangerous, as shown in 1 Samuel 6:19–20 and 2 Samuel 6:6–7.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The men of the Gershonite clan (see Numbers 3:21–26) were responsible for general service and carrying loads (Numbers 4:24). They handled the curtains, coverings, ropes, and related equipment. These were less central to Israel's worship. The duties of the Gershonites focused on the Tent of Meeting in general. This was unlike the Kohathites, who were responsible for the holy objects of the inner place of worship.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This assignment to the Merarite clan involved items of lower priority than those of the Kohathites and Gershonites. It had to be done in a specific way, with each man's load assigned by name (Numbers 4:32; see also 1 Corinthians 14:40). The Gershonites and Merarites did not have the status of Kohath’s family. Yet, each group helped move and set up the Tent of Meeting.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The numbering and recording the Levites' names and ensuring each man understood his task was crucial. This helped properly organize Israel for travel and camping and protected the Tent of Meeting.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Modern Western people may find it difficult to understand the Old Testament laws of purity. Today, things like skin diseases, bodily discharges, or contact with a dead body are viewed mainly as health concerns. But in the Old Testament, the main concern was protecting God’s holiness from ceremonial uncleanness (see Leviticus 11–15). 

The community had to keep the camp holy. Nothing unclean could touch what belonged to the Lord (Numbers 5:2–3). They had to choose between having God in the camp or allowing a ceremonially polluted person stay. Both could not remain (Numbers 5:3). 

• The importance of purity continues from Leviticus and Numbers to the book of Revelation. Nothing ceremonially unclean will enter the New Jerusalem where God lives (see study note on Revelation 21:27). In the New Testament, impurity most often refers to what is morally impure (Acts 10:28; Ephesians 5:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: These laws speak about cleanliness, repayment, and staying faithful in marriage.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
These legal matters were meant to protect the purity of the Israelites, their priests, and the tabernacle. Purity here refers to being clean and set apart for worship.

These rules helped the people remember who they were. Israel was a theocracy (a nation ruled directly by God). God was their true king.

Moses served as God’s main spokesman. Through him, God gave laws and instructions to the people.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• skin disease: The Hebrew word here describes various, contagious skin diseases (compare Leviticus 13–14). 

• bodily discharge: This refers to fluids associated with sexual organs (Leviticus 15; compare Luke 8:43–48). 

• a dead person: See Numbers 6:6–11; Numbers 19:11.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The laws about confession and restitution show the strong Hebrew concern for moral behavior (Leviticus 6:1–7).

Confession means admitting one’s sin before God. Restitution means making things right by repaying what was taken or damaged. A person who wronged another had to return what was stolen and often add more as a penalty.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Harming another person is also betraying the Lord (literally to act unfaithful in unfaithfulness; compare Leviticus 5:8). Being right with God leads to being right with others. If we treat others wrongly, it shows our relationship with the Lord is not right.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This restitution and the guilt offering for the sin were intended to teach personal responsibility to live holy with God (see Leviticus 6–7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Since sin is ultimately against God, the one doing wrong must make restitution to the LORD (Leviticus 5:6; Psalm 51:4). God allowed the human victims of the sin to receive this payment. If no victims were alive, the priest would receive the payment on behalf of the LORD. Those doing wrong must also offer a valuable sacrifice to restore their ceremonial purity and their relationship with God (Numbers 5:1–4). 

• the atonement is made for him: See study note on Leviticus 1:4.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Priests partially supported their families by receiving a share of the sacrifices. Sometimes, they could sell extra sacrifices to fund the priesthood, maintain the sanctuary, and help with other religious needs (see 1 Corinthians 8:4–13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
This detailed test for adultery, a "trial by ordeal," is the only one in the Old Testament. Yet, trial by ordeal was common in the ancient Near East. God had a special interest in protecting marriage. It was the foundation of Hebrew society. 

The ordeal was intended to promote marital faithfulness. We do not know how often such ordeals actually happened. This procedure relied on God to intervene so that justice occurred when evidence was lacking (see 1 Corinthians 5:5).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The husband presented his case to the priest, and the “law of jealousy” (Numbers 5:29) transferred the husband's jealousy and suspicion to a higher court of appeal.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The holy water and the dust were sacred because of their association with the sanctuary.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell: Thigh is a polite way to speak about the reproductive organs (compare Genesis 24:2; Genesis 47:29). Something would stop her ability to have children. The punishment matched the crime, as sexual immorality led to infertility.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The image of drinking curses appears again in Ezekiel 2:8–3:3 and Revelation 10:8–11.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The law describes a trial by ordeal (a test in which God was asked to show guilt or innocence). In this case, a husband could bring his wife to the priest if he suspected adultery.

The summary of the law makes one point clear. If the husband raised questions about his wife’s guilt or innocence, he was not considered guilty simply for asking.

Some readers may notice what seems like a double standard. Ancient laws often focused on the woman’s failure in cases of adultery. This pattern was common in the ancient world.

However, Israel’s legal system did not excuse the man involved. The law required punishment for both parties in an affair (as in Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:21–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The voluntary vow of a Nazirite allowed men or women to separate themselves to the LORD. The Nazirite lifestyle varied throughout Hebrew history. People took vows seriously in ancient times as a way to show devotion or gratitude to God. This vow could be temporary or permanent. It involved avoiding alcoholic drinks, not cutting hair, and avoiding contact with corpses. 

Nazirite restrictions allowed members of non-Levitical tribes to have a more demanding and highly respected relationship with God. The Nazirite vow is probably best known because of Samson (Judges 13–16). See also 1 Samuel 1:11; Jeremiah 35; Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23–26; compare Luke 1:15.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Nazirite: The Hebrew word nazir comes from a verb meaning "to separate."

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The law required priests to avoid drinking wine before serving in the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 10:9). The Nazirite vow allowed non-Levites to extend this rule. They avoided wine everywhere, at all times, and anything from a grapevine.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: hair: This had a special symbolic meaning (see Leviticus 19:27). Religious people often left their hair uncut or shaved it completely (Numbers 8:5–7). The Israelites did not have to leave their hair completely uncut, but the Nazirites did.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Touching dead bodies made people ceremonially unclean (Numbers 9:6–10). Priests could only touch the dead bodies of close relatives (Leviticus 21:1–4). But Nazirites could not touch any dead body at all.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The law gave instructions for restoring purity after unavoidable contact with a dead body. Contact with a dead body made a person ceremonially unclean (not fit for worship for a period of time). The person had to follow certain steps in order to be restored.

Special procedures and offerings also marked the end of a Nazirite vow. A Nazirite vow was a special promise to set oneself apart for God for a period of time. When the time ended, the person brought sacrifices and completed the required rituals.

The law also gives a strong warning about fulfilling the vow (Numbers 6:21). A person who made such a promise had to complete it fully. God expected faithfulness in keeping vows made to him.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The priestly blessing connects to the themes of worship and purity in chapters Numbers 5:5–6. It is a prayer where priests ask for God's blessings for Israel. As representatives of God, priests had the duty to pray (compare Leviticus 9:23; Deuteronomy 10:8). This prayer is similar to the high priestly prayer of Jesus in John 17.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The first half of this verse asks for blessings like health, wealth, and fertility. 

The second half seeks protection from all kinds of dangers. This prayer is similar to the language in Psalms 121:3–8; Psalms 140:4; and 141:9. These sincere requests are still good examples for prayer and blessings that people can seek for everyone. The entire poem emphasizes the Lord as the source of all good things.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Psalm 67:1 has a short version of this blessing. This is similar to one found on a silver amulet from Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem’s Old City. A second, larger silver amulet from the same tomb has the full blessing with words almost the same as here. 

The Second Temple period lasted from Ezra to the time of Jesus. Priests would give a blessing at each day's sacrifice or at the end of services. This blessing is still used in Jewish and Christian liturgy (the formal order of prayers and worship, as in Numbers 6:27).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you: This is a desire for God's approval. 

• be gracious to you: God's people need his grace and mercy in a dangerous world (compare Psalms 31:16; Psalms 67:1; Psalms 80:3, Psalms 80:7, Psalms 80:19).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God's favor, shown through his countenance or face, means his approval and special attention (compare Psalm 30:7). Divine peace (Hebrew shalom) is more than only the absence of conflict or violence. God's peace brings complete well-being, health, and wholeness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The priests were mediators of God’s covenant with Israel. A mediator is someone who stands between two parties to represent them. The priests stood between God and the people.

Their duty was to pray for the people. They also spoke God’s blessing over them. In this way, they helped maintain the covenant relationship between God and Israel (see Romans 8:34; Hebrews 2:17–18; Hebrews 4:14–16). He intercedes for believers, which means he prays for them before God. As the great high priest, he brings his people into God’s presence and secures God’s blessing for them.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Moses set up the tabernacle on the first day of the second year after the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 40:1–2). 

• Moses finished setting up the tabernacle. Then he anointed and consecrated it and all its furnishings, along with the altar and all its utensils (compare Exodus 40:9–10; Leviticus 8:10–11). The altar, as the place of sacrifice, was especially important among the holy furniture.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This is a detailed description of the offerings made by Israel's 12 tribes during the dedication of the tabernacle. They dedicated these gifts for 12 days.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The same tribal leaders who helped with the registration in chapter Numbers 1:1 also appear in Numbers 7:2–3. The non-Levitical tribes gave the Gershonites and Merarites wagons and oxen to move the heavy parts of the tabernacle and other items (see chapter Numbers 4:4). 

• These vehicles and animals were the first offerings from the Hebrew tribes (Numbers 7:2). The tribal leaders also presented these practical gifts along with the more elaborate offerings they dedicated (Numbers 7:10, Numbers 7:12–83).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Later, the Israelites tried to move the ark of the covenant using a cart, but it ended tragically (1 Samuel 6:8, 1 Samuel 6:11; 2 Samuel 6:3, 2 Samuel 6:6–7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: When they anointed the altar, the tribal leaders gave the wagons and oxen, silver and gold vessels, and other religious offerings for the altar. Starting with the tribe of Judah, the leaders brought these gifts to the tabernacle for 12 days. They collected these gifts from the Egyptians when Israel left Egypt (compare Exodus 12:35–36; Exodus 25:3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
One by one, the tribal leaders brought their gifts for the dedication of the altar. Each tribe participated until the whole Hebrew confederation (the united group of twelve tribes) had taken part.

The text repeats the description of each tribe’s gift. This repetition highlights the shared nature of the ceremony. Every tribe had a role in setting apart their place of worship for God.

The careful listing of the gifts may reflect detailed record keeping, like an archive or ledger (an official written record). The text notes that the silver bowls and plates contained grain offerings. The gold dishes held incense.

Each tribe also brought animals for a burnt offering, a sin offering, and a peace offering, as required in Leviticus. These offerings showed worship, repentance, and fellowship with God.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This paragraph first summarizes the gifts and offerings from each tribe. Then it lists expensive containers, offerings, incense, and sacrificial animals. These large and costly gifts showed the importance of the altar, the tabernacle, and the God who was served there. The law required these sacrifices, but the Hebrews gave the special gifts generously.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• After dedicating the Tent of Meeting (the tabernacle) and setting it apart as holy, it became the center of divine revelation. There, Moses spoke with God, who revealed his will and presence (Leviticus 16:2, Leviticus 16:13–17). This communication came from the ark of the covenant. It was specifically between the two cherubim above the ark's cover, also called "the mercy seat" (compare Exodus 25:17–22). 

• For the Israelites, this was the special place for atonement, similar to the significance in the Christian faith of the cross where Jesus died (see Hebrews 9–10, especially Hebrews 9:5). God's voice, heard by Moses the mediator, fulfilled the promise in Exodus 25:22 and Numbers 30:6. The Lord's presence ensured the holiness of Israel's wilderness place of worship.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
These verses give specific instructions for placing the lampstand (Hebrew menorah) in the tabernacle. The lampstand (see Exodus 25:31–40). It was made with branches shaped like a stylized tree.

The inside of the tabernacle had no windows, so it was dark. The light from the lampstand helped the priests carry out their duties.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord gave instructions for the dedication and cleansing of the Levites. The Levites were set apart to serve in the tabernacle.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The ceremony to make the Levites ceremonially clean involved sprinkling with water, shaving all hair, and wearing clean clothes. This was similar to ceremonies for cleansing from ceremonial impurity. 

• water of purification: This phrase appears only here. The sprinkling symbolized washing away sin and had symbolic importance similar to later Jewish washings and Christian baptism. This water might have been the same as the mixture with ashes from the red heifer that removed sin (see Numbers 19:9; also Hebrews 9:13). 

• Shaving their entire body was also part of being declared ceremonially clean from the ceremonial impurity of polluting diseases (Leviticus 14:8). 

• Washing clothes was part of all cleansing from ceremonial impurity (for example, Leviticus 15:5–27).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: laying their hands on them: Israel acknowledged the Levites' special status and offered them as their representatives in the presence of the Lord (Numbers 8:16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The mention of Aaron's raised hands suggests that Israel offered the Levites to the Lord as a wave offering. Priests would lift up this type of offering to the Lord (compare Leviticus 7:30). The Levites committed themselves to tasks that made them living and holy sacrifices (compare Romans 12:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Levites offered the right sacrifices before doing their work in the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 8:15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: A plague was an appropriate punishment for unlawful actions (Numbers 11:33; Numbers 14:37).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• These are guidelines for the length of the Levites' service. 

• Whereas Numbers 4:3 says their service in the Tent of Meeting started at age 30, Numbers 8:24 says age 25. This difference might show changes in age requirements over time, depending on how many Levite men were available. Those aged 25–29 might have been unofficial workers or apprentices. 

• Both passages set the retirement age at 50. Retired Levites could serve as guards of the Tent of Meeting (see Psalm 84:10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: A year after Israel left Egypt, it was time for them to celebrate their second Passover in the Sinai wilderness. Those unable to celebrate at the set time could do so a month later.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• God told the Hebrews to celebrate Passover at the set time (see Exodus 12:6). 

• at twilight: The Hebrew day starts at sunset.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: When it was time to celebrate Passover, some men could not participate due to the rules in Leviticus 7:20–21. They wanted to follow the rules, but it seemed impossible for them.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses agreed to ask the Lord about this difficult case (compare Numbers 7:89).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God's solution to the problem was to allow a makeup ceremony one month later for two special cases (see also 2 Chronicles 30:2 Chronicles 30). Yet, he warned the Israelites not to neglect the Passover and to celebrate it according to the rules.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites could not break the bones of the Passover lamb (see Exodus 12:46; Psalm 34:20; John 19:32–36; compare John 1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7). The apostle John mentioned this instruction when he wrote that they did not break the legs of Jesus when he was on the cross (John 19:36).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
If a person refused to observe the required Passover, that person was to be cut off from the community. The Passover was a central act of worship that remembered God’s rescue of Israel from Egypt.

The phrase “cut off” can have more than one meaning in the Old Testament. It may refer to the death penalty. It may also mean banishment from the community (being removed from the people). The exact meaning in this case is not fully clear (see study note on Leviticus 7:20–21).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Foreigners who lived among the Hebrews and wanted to celebrate the Passover could do so by following the same laws, but circumcision was required for males who desired to eat the Passover meal (see also Exodus 12:48–49).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This passage is similar to Exodus 40:17, Exodus 40:34–38. It gives more details about how God used the pillar of cloud and fire to lead his people (see also Exodus 13:21–22). The Lord was faithful and clearly guided his people in the wilderness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Even Israel's enemies saw the fiery cloud (Numbers 14:14). This clearly represented God's glorious presence and the way he guided their movement.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Israel needed clear signals so the tribes could receive instructions. Two silver trumpets provided a simple and effective way to signal all the tribes to move. 

• These trumpets were not the ram’s horns (Hebrew shofar) often mentioned in the Old Testament (for example, Joshua 6:4–6). Israelite craftsmen made them from hammered silver brought out of Egypt.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: They used the two trumpets to alert people for important announcements (compare Revelation 8–11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: When it was time to journey to the next destination, the trumpets sounded to signal when to camp and when to move. This sound was in addition to the movement of the pillar of cloud (compare Numbers 9:15–22 and chapter Numbers 2:2).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the priests, are to sound the trumpets: They used these trumpets only for matters related to God and his rule over Israel, which the priests served.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The trumpets marked holy events that people might not easily recognize. Trumpets that called to battle would remind the Lord to save the Hebrews from their enemies (Hosea 5:8; Joel 2:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Leaving Sinai was a key moment in Israel's history. The Israelites now had the law and God would test them on how they obeyed it. The departure from Sinai marked the start of the march toward Canaan, although it became a long journey (compare Deuteronomy 1:6–8, Deuteronomy 1:19). This passage summarizes the daily routines during the journey.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Israelites traveled to the wilderness of Paran. This region was dry and harsh. It was either arid or semi-arid, which means it received very little rain.

The wilderness of Paran lay in the northeastern part of the Sinai Peninsula. It was south of the Negev and west of the Dead Sea and the Arabah Rift (a long valley that runs from the Dead Sea southward; compare Genesis 21:21).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The order of march described here is different from Numbers 2:3–34. There, all three Levitical clans carried the tabernacle and its furnishings in the center of the camp. They marched between the groups led by Judah and Reuben, and the groups led by Ephraim and Dan.

In this passage, the arrangement is more detailed. The Gershonites and Merarites carried the structural parts of the tabernacle between Judah and Reuben. The Kohathites carried the most sacred furniture between Reuben and Ephraim.

This arrangement was practical. It gave the Gershonites and Merarites time to set up the tabernacle before the Kohathites arrived with the sacred objects. This plan also provided protection for the holy items.

In addition, this pattern spread the Levites among the tribes. Their presence among the people may have strengthened spiritual influence throughout the camp (compare Matthew 13:33; Matthew 16:6, Matthew 16:11–12; 1 Corinthians 5:6–7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• After the journey toward Paran began, Moses asked his brother-in-law, Hobab, to guide the Israelites (literally and you will serve for us for eyes) (compare Judges 4:11). In this way, Hobab would share in their promised blessings. As a Midianite shepherd, Hobab knew the routes and possible sources of food and water in the Sinai Peninsula. 

• Reuel the Midianite: See “Jethro (Reuel)” Profile. 

• my own land and my own people: Midian was probably in northwestern Arabia. Judges 1:16 suggests that Hobab accepted the request.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the mountain of the LORD: Here, this refers to Mount Sinai. In other places, it means Mount Moriah or Zion in Jerusalem (Genesis 22:14; Psalm 24:3; Isaiah 2:3; Zechariah 8:3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: When the ark of the covenant set out, Moses called on the Lord as a warrior. He acknowledged the Lord would help Israel win the promised land and fight their battles (compare Psalm 68:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This invocation (formal call for God’s help) asked the Lord to be present with his people. It was spoken when the Israelites set out or camped.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Soon the people began to complain … fire from the LORD blazed: The link between Israel’s complaints and God’s punishment is a major theme in Numbers and throughout the Old Testament (for example, Deuteronomy 9:22; Psalm 78). God is holy and just, and he demands obedience from his people. Complaints are the same as rejecting him (compare Numbers 11:20). 

• their hardship: Mount Sinai had been a stable home for a year. The journey to Paran brought heat, thirst, and fatigue. 

• consumed the outskirts of the camp: Compare Leviticus 10:2.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This is one of many occasions in the wilderness when Israel was disobedient to the Lord.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The people asked Moses to speak to God again on their behalf. This stopped the fire of God's judgment (compare Exodus 15:25; Exodus 32:11–14). 

• Taberah: Compare Numbers 11:34–35; see Deuteronomy 9:22.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Who will feed us meat?: The Israelites had flocks and herds (for example, Numbers 32:1; Exodus 12:32, Exodus 12:38; Exodus 17:3; Exodus 34:3). But the animals were more valuable for their dairy products and other benefits while alive. They only butchered them for meat occasionally. The Hebrews did not have enough meat to regularly feed such a large population (compare Numbers 11:21–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Israel had not given up the attitude that led to judgment at Taberah (Numbers 11:1–3). At Taberah, the people complained, and the Lord sent fire among them.

Soon after, they joined the foreign rabble (a mixed group of non-Israelites who had left Egypt with them) in craving the foods of Egypt. They longed for the fish, vegetables, and other foods they had known there.

In doing this, they forgot the suffering and slavery they had experienced in Egypt. They remembered the food but ignored the hardship.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord had earlier provided manna and quail (Exodus 16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: People often explain manna as a naturally occurring edible substance (but see Deuteronomy 8:3). Yet, its amount and how long it lasted was miraculous.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Israelites' constant complaining frustrated Moses, leading him to express his own complaints to God. With extreme sarcasm, Moses reminded God that he had not wanted this responsibility (compare Exodus 4:10). Israel became such a burden that Moses wished God would do him the favor of ending his life (compare Job 6:9). 

• Moses' complaint was acceptable, unlike the people's complaints, because he sought the Lord instead of longing for Egypt's pleasures.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Jethro suggested that Moses should have different levels of judges (Exodus 18:13–26). He focused on practical issues like the tribal leaders who helped Moses with the registration (Numbers 1:5–15). 

In contrast, the group of 70 elders would give Israel spiritual guidance. They needed a share of God's Spirit. Moses already had this, and it made him the Lord's special spokesman. Their ability to lead depended on God's Spirit being with them (compare 1 Samuel 10:6; 1 Samuel 19:20; Joel 2:28; Acts 2:16–18; 1 Corinthians 12:10; 2 Peter 1:20–21).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The text does not describe what happened when the Spirit rested on them and they prophesied. It only says that they spoke as the Spirit enabled them.

Whatever took place, it may have included ecstatic speech (intense or Spirit-driven words spoken in a special way). Similar events appear later in Acts 2:4 and 1 Corinthians 14:2. However, the text suggests that this was a unique event.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Joshua’s worthy jealousy was a desire to safeguard his master’s status. But, Moses was humble and did not feel threatened by Eldad and Medad's prophecy (Numbers 12:3). Instead, he was glad to see God working through others in special ways. Moses had leadership qualities that the younger Joshua had not yet developed (compare Mark 9:38–40).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God answered the people's complaints by sending a storm of quail and a plague. God had given quail with manna in Exodus 16:13. But here the quail showed God's judgment through an excessive abundance.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The exact locations of Kibroth-hattaavah and Hazeroth are unknown.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Most interpreters believe the Cushite woman is Zipporah, the wife of Moses. She was from Midian (Exodus 2:16–22). They see Cush as referring to Cushan, a region and people near Midian (Habakkuk 3:7). 

Other interpreters think Cushite refers to Kusi in northern Arabia, Ethiopia, or Sudan. This would suggest she was a different wife. 

In either case, it is possible that Miriam and Aaron disapproved of his having married a non-Israelite or that they were jealous of her influence over Moses.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Miriam and Aaron may have seen the marriage of Moses as a threat to their status and goals. The verses list Miriam first, suggesting she started this family conflict. This could explain why God punished her and not Aaron (Numbers 12:9–10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Rebellion did not come only from the “rabble” or from the Israelites who were tired of manna (Numbers 11:4). It also came from within the family of Moses.

Aaron the high priest and Miriam the prophetess spoke against Moses (Exodus 29:30; Exodus 15:20). Their actions showed that even Israel’s spiritual leaders struggled with jealousy and doubt.

At this time, Israel was moving toward a lowest point in its rebellion against God (Numbers 13:25–14:12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Challenging the authority of Moses meant rejecting the Lord's choice of him as Israel's leader. 

• the LORD heard this: The same phrase in Numbers 11:1 hints at the Lord's response.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The humility of Moses stands in sharp contrast to the jealousy of Miriam and Aaron. The text says that Moses was very humble. His character reflected a godly spirit (see also Proverbs 3:34; Matthew 5:5). 

• The statement about the humility of Moses appears as a parenthetical comment (a brief note inserted into the story). It presents the truth from God’s point of view.

Some think these words may have been written by Moses. Others believe they may have been added later by an editor. In either case, the comment highlights the faithful and humble character of Moses.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: In response to this rebellion, the Lord spoke directly. He reaffirmed the special status and authority of Moses.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord trusted Moses, leading to a close relationship. God communicated with prophets through visions and dreams, but he spoke to Moses face to face (literally mouth to mouth; see Exodus 33:8–11, Exodus 33:18–23; Deuteronomy 34:10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Miriam experienced the burning anger of the Lord (see study note on 12:1–2). When Aaron saw what happened to her, he confessed their sin and asked Moses to pray for them (compare Numbers 11:2). Both Moses and the Lord accepted Aaron's confession.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Miriam had to follow the usual steps to become ceremonially pure after a skin disease (Numbers 5:2–4; Leviticus 13–14).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The camp in the Wilderness of Paran was at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 13:26; Deuteronomy 1:19–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses chose a leader from each tribe to explore the land God promised to the Hebrews. The tribes listed are from chapter Numbers 1:1, but the order is different. Caleb and Joshua later prove to be men of faith (Numbers 14:30).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Twelve spies explored the fertile land of Canaan and found strong enemies defending it. Earlier chapters show Israel's disobedience, hinting at future failures. The Israelites did not have the obedience, courage, or faith to capture the land. So, the Lord made them spend 40 years in the Wilderness of Sinai. That generation did not receive their inheritance in the promised land.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The scouting mission had a clear military purpose. The spies also needed to gather information about natural resources and food. These things were concerning to the Israelites since they left Egypt (chapter Numbers 11:11; Exodus 16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The season for harvesting the first ripe grapes came in late July or August, during the summer.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The distance from the Wilderness of Zin to Lebo-hamath in Syria was about 275 miles. The Wilderness of Zin was between the wilderness of Paran and Canaan's southern border see Numbers 34:3–5; Joshua 15:1–4). Lebo-hamath means "entrance of Hamath." This could refer to a mountain pass or a city near Hamath. 

• The exact location of Rehob is unclear. But it was probably the same as Old Testament Beth-rehob, near a major route to Hamath. This text outlines the approximate borders of the promised land (see 1 Kings 8:65). The phrase from Dan to Beersheba often marked Israel’s traditional boundaries (Judges 20:1; 2 Samuel 3:10). It covered a smaller area than the territory explored by Israel’s spies.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The spies explored the land of Canaan. In contrast to the Sinai wilderness, it was rich and fertile.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Israel's spies traveled into Canaan's hill country through the Negev, the dry southern region near the wilderness of Zin. In the southern part of Canaan's central hill country, they reached Hebron. This was where Israel's ancestors had lived (Genesis 13:18; Genesis 23:19; Genesis 35:27; Genesis 37:14). 

• The descendants of Anak were famous for their size and strength (for example, Deuteronomy 9:2). 

• Zoan (later called Tanis by the Greeks) was a famous city in Egypt's eastern delta (see also Psalms 78:12, Psalms 78:43; Isaiah 19:11–13; Isaiah 30:3–5).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The spies agreed the land was good, but most doubted Israel could conquer it. The strong and well-fed Canaanites had built fortified towns for protection.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Kadesh is often linked to ‘Ain el-Qudeirat, a spring at the northern border of Sinai and the southern edge of Canaan. There is no evidence of a Hebrew camp there during the exodus or the wilderness wanderings. So, some scholars have suggested that ancient Kadesh was in a different location.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The promised land is also known as land flowing with milk and honey. In biblical times, milk and dairy were key parts of the diet. Milk symbolized abundance (see Deuteronomy 32:14; Isaiah 55:1; Joel 3:18). Honey added sweetness (see Psalms 19:10; Psalms 119:103; Ezekiel 3:3; Revelation 10:9–10). The phrase describes a desirable place with plenty of food and resources (compare Numbers 16:13–14; see also Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 6:3; Deuteronomy 26:15; Jeremiah 11:4–5; Ezekiel 20:6). 

The New Testament emphasizes the spiritual nature of God's promises, pointing to a promised inheritance in heaven (see Romans 9:6–8; Galatians 6:14–16; Revelation 21:1–2).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The spies answer the question of Numbers 13:18. Many ethnic groups lived in ancient Canaan.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Caleb and Joshua (see Numbers 14:6, Numbers 14:10, Numbers 14:30) gave a more positive report about the land than the other spies did (compare Numbers 14:31–33).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Nephilim: See the study note on Genesis 6:4.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The people rejected the testimony of the faithful spies, Joshua and Caleb. Then rebellion spread throughout the community. Moses intervened to save Israel from total destruction. Those who disobeyed God died during a 40-year journey in the wilderness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The threats they complained about were real, but the Israelites should have trusted the Lord. In the ancient Near East, victors often took wives and children as plunder after battles. 

• go back to Egypt: The Israelites quickly forgot their slavery and the difficulties of the wilderness (Exodus 2:23–24; Numbers 11:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses and Aaron bowed down to show humility, fear, grief, and anguish.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Joshua and Caleb tried to stop the rebellion and prevent God's punishment. They tore their clothing to show their sorrow.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Joshua and Caleb realized that Israel's lack of courage and criticism of Moses and Aaron were acts of rebellion against the Lord. They knew the consequences of this rebellion. 

• the LORD is with us: This was the source of their confidence (compare Romans 8:31).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Joshua and Caleb encouraged trust in God, which led to more opposition. The protests against the leaders turned into threats against the faithful spies. All the Israelites' objections stopped suddenly. This was because the glory (Hebrew kabod) of the LORD appeared at the Tent of Meeting, the site of divine communication (see Exodus 24:15–18; Ezekiel 1) .

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God seemed amazed that Israel still did not trust him. This was despite his miraculous rescue from slavery and provision for their needs in the wilderness (see Deuteronomy 4:32–40; Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
God is patient, but he will not tolerate open rebellion from his people (see Exodus 32:7–10). 

In the New Testament, the writer of Hebrews mentions this event to strengthen the faith of Christians whose trust in the gospel was weakening (Hebrews 3:7–19; Hebrews 12:3, Hebrews 12:25; see also Psalm 95:8–11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses spoke to God on behalf of his people. He reminded God that his reputation related to Israel's. He pleaded for God to continue his faithfulness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses had used this argument before when he asked for forgiveness for Israel's rebellion (Exodus 32:10–14). Moses knew God would still punish the Israelites (Deuteronomy 7:9–10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Since leaving Egypt, Israel’s history had been marked by repeated transgressions (acts of disobedience; chapters Numbers 11:11–12; Exodus 15:22–27; Exodus 17:1–7; Exodus 32:1–14; Leviticus 10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Because Moses argued with God, God forgave Israel's rebellion and did not destroy them. Yet, the stubborn generation of adults would never see the promised land.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The people did not obey or have faith because they refused to listen to God's voice. They had seen the Lord's glory and miraculous signs (see study note on 14:10; Exodus 4:29–31; Exodus 7:1–11:10; Exodus 14:15–31; Exodus 16:1–17:13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• After leaving the promised land, God told the Israelites to march in the opposite direction. 

• The Red Sea could refer to bodies of water on either side of the Sinai Peninsula (the Gulf of Aqaba or the Gulf of Suez).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel’s disobedience brought on the consequences they feared would come from obeying.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• each day: Compare Numbers 13:25. 

• My alienation: Compare Ezekiel 5:8; Ezekiel 21:3.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The threat of divine punishment for their sins caused the people of Israel to feel grief. Yet, their wills remained rebellious, and they disobeyed the Lord's command again (Numbers 14:25). Caleb and Joshua's based their initial confidence on God's promise to be with them (Numbers 14:9). Yet, God would not fight with the Israelites until all the rebels had died.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Because you have turned away from the LORD, He will not be with you: The prediction of Moses summarizes the entire chapter.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The ark of the covenant represented God's presence and blessings (compare 1 Samuel 4:1–11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Hormah means "destruction" in Hebrew (see Numbers 21:1–3 for reference).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: These instructions suggest that the Israelites would eventually live in the promised land (Numbers 14:31; Numbers 15:18).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Chapters Numbers 1:1–14 cover a short time period, but chapter Numbers 15:15 marks the start of a long period. This is the main part of the forty years in the wilderness, about which little is known. There are references to events during this time (for example, Deuteronomy 8:2–6; Deuteronomy 29:5–6; Joshua 5:4–8; Ezekiel 20:10–26; Amos 5:25–26; Acts 7:42–43). 

During this period, Moses continued to give laws to guide Israel’s life as a nation. These laws would be especially important in the future. They were meant for the day when the people who survived the wilderness would enter the promised land. 

This chapter addresses three main types of laws. Numbers 15 is in the middle of stories about a stubborn and disobedient Israel. It offers hope that the promised land still waited for the next generation of Israel’s people.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: an offering … a pleasing aroma to the LORD: Honor and thanks through sacrifices and offerings pleases God.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: All people in the land, both Israelites and foreigners, were to be equal before the Lord in all matters (see also Leviticus 24:22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
These gifts were signs of gratitude to God for the crops he provided. The people were not to give these offerings right away. They were to begin after the Hebrews reached the promised land.

At that time, they would settle there and begin planting crops. Then they would bring these gifts to thank God for the harvest.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Sins done without knowing were treated differently from sins done on purpose (Numbers 15:30–31). The law also made a difference between the actions of the whole community and the actions of one person (see also Leviticus 4–5).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Atonement (the way God provides forgiveness and restores a relationship with him) could be made for sins done without knowing or by accident (Numbers 15:22–29). However, a person who sinned openly and proudly was treated differently (literally with a high hand; compare Exodus 14:8). Such a person showed open disrespect toward God. This was considered blasphemy (speaking against God in a dishonoring way). That person had to face serious consequences (compare Leviticus 24:10–16; see also Deuteronomy 17:2–6; Hebrews 10:26–31). 

• cut off from among his people: See study notes on Exodus 31:14–15; Leviticus 7:20–21.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This story gives an example of what Numbers 15:30–31 teaches. The Sabbath was the Lord’s holy day. The people were not allowed to ignore it or treat it as unimportant (Exodus 20:8–11; Exodus 31:14–15; Exodus 35:1–3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Although it was clear that the man was guilty, the community might have been unsure about his punishment. The death sentence was appropriate because ignoring the Sabbath showed a rejection of God's gracious covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:12–17). It was similar to blasphemy (Numbers 15:30; Leviticus 24:10–16; compare 1 Timothy 1:20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• If the Hebrews had remembered their special relationship with the Lord, they might have avoided the problems in Numbers. The tassels reminded Israel of their unique bond with a holy God and his expectations. He had freed his people from Egypt. Consistent with his call to a covenant relationship, he expected them to observe the law (see Deuteronomy 6:6–9; Matthew 9:20; Matthew 14:36; Matthew 23:5). 

• The color blue was a sign of royalty, which means kingship or rule. It also reminded the people of God’s holiness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Another rebellion demanded a clear separation of duties between priests and Levites. This power struggle was more serious than previous rebellions against God's authority (chapter Numbers 11:11; Numbers 12:1–15; Numbers 14:1–45). 

In these historical events, the rebels protested minor issues and questioned their leaders' actions. Yet, Moses reminded them that they were actually rebelling against God. As a result, the Israelites suffered deadly consequences for their rebellion.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The rebels "envied Moses, as well as Aaron" (Psalm 106:16). They claimed Moses and Aaron had overstepped their authority because all Israelites were God's chosen people (Exodus 19:6). Their protest for equality against Moses and Aaron's authority probably intended to replace it with their own.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses … fell facedown on the ground to pray (compare Numbers 14:5; Numbers 16:22). Then he challenged Korah and his followers to a test.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Take censers: Korah and his group were to act like priests by burning incense (as in Leviticus 16:11–13). By doing this, they were claiming the right to serve as priests. God himself would decide who truly had the right to serve in that role.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Chapters Numbers 3:3–4 describe the special ministry duties of the Levites. Aaron's descendants had the priesthood (Numbers 3:1–4). The rebels complained against the Lord, not Moses or Aaron.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
land flowing with milk and honey: This phrase repeats the words the spies used earlier to describe Canaan (Numbers 13:27). In this story, however, the words are used with sarcasm.

The speakers twist the meaning on purpose. They use this phrase to describe Egypt in a positive way. This distorts the truth about life in Egypt, where the Israelites had lived as slaves (see study note on 11:4–15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Israelites were leaving their new homeland because they had rebelled against Moses. He had done everything possible to bring them to that land (chapters Numbers 13:13–14). 

• Will you gouge out the eyes of these men?: They accused Moses and Aaron of trying to mislead the Israelites.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Do not regard their offering: Compare Psalm 109:7 and Proverbs 28:9.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses gave final instructions for a test to see if the Lord would accept the rebels' offering or Aaron's offering.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: At the height of the rebellion, the Lord intervened to save Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron then prayed for the people.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: had gathered his whole assembly … at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting: This was either to watch the test or to remove Moses and Aaron from leadership.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord threatened to destroy the entire community because of widespread sin (compare Genesis 18:16–33). Moses and Aaron prayed to limit the Lord's judgment to those guilty of this specific rebellion.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Do not touch anything that belongs to them: These men and their belongings were now "set apart for destruction" (see Leviticus 27:28–29; compare Deuteronomy 7:26; Deuteronomy 13:17; Joshua 6:18; Joshua 7:1–26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Moses believed that God would deliver justice, and God did so (Numbers 16:31–35; compare 1 Kings 18:18–40). 

• into Sheol: This was the place of the dead in the Old Testament. Sheol describes the realm where people go after death (see 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Samuel 22:5–6; Job 3:20–22; Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27–33; 1 Corinthians 15:15; Revelation 20:13–14).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Korah’s sons did not die at this time (Numbers 26:10–11). Later, his descendants became gatekeepers and musicians in the temple (1 Chronicles 9:19, 1 Chronicles 9:31; 1 Chronicles 26:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19; see the titles of Psalms 42; Psalms 45:45–49; Psalms 84:84–85; Psalms 87:87–88).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The 250 Israelite leaders tried to offer incense even though they were not priests. Their fate was like that of Nadab and Abihu, who also offered unauthorized fire before the Lord (Leviticus 10:1–2). They also shared the same judgment as those who complained about the hardships in the wilderness (Numbers 11:1; compare 2 Kings 1:10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Although the men who used the incense burners were wicked, the vessels themselves were holy and had to be treated with care and respect. The burning coals were also holy and had to be scattered so that they would not be used for any other purpose.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Eleazar made a bronze sheet to cover the altar, replacing or adding to the earlier one (Exodus 38:2). Like the plain blue tassels in Numbers 15:37–41, it reminded the people of Israel to obey God.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites continued their self-destructive and defiant behavior, which caused their problems. They then blamed Moses and Aaron for the events.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The glory of the LORD appeared again and threatened to destroy the people of Israel (see Numbers 16:19–20). Moses and Aaron intervened by falling facedown on the ground.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses and Aaron quickly acted to save the Israelites from God's anger. Aaron used an incense burner with hot coals among the people to stop the plague.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The shepherd's staff was a common item (see Psalm 23:4). Like the scepter, it symbolized authority (see Jeremiah 48:17). This trial was fitting because the Hebrew words for "staffs" and "tribes" sound the same. The Lord's chosen staff would show his chosen tribe.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord gave another test to make the lesson clear. This test repeated the teaching from the events in chapter Numbers 16:16. It also prepared the people for the instructions that follow in chapter Numbers 18:18.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The staffs were in the Lord's presence, a safe place where no one could interfere with them (Numbers 17:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Aaron’s staff … produced almonds: This proved he was God's chosen leader and that the Levites had a special role. The cups on the lampstand of the Tent of the Testimony (the tabernacle) had the shape of almond blossoms (Exodus 25:33–36). Later, the prophet Jeremiah’s vision of an almond branch symbolized the Lord's watchfulness and his plans to act (Jeremiah 1:11–12). 

• There is no natural reason for Aaron’s staff to bud. Almond wood is soft when alive and only hardens enough for use as a staff after it has dried.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: After each tribal leader claimed his staff, it was clear that Aaron’s deserved special treatment. They placed it permanently in front of the ark of the covenant to warn potential rebels. It would also warn Israelites who complained about the Lord and his appointed leaders. The ark of the covenant eventually contained this staff, a jar of manna, and the stone tablets of the law (compare Hebrews 9:4). This was to remind the Israelites of their time wandering in the wilderness.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord and his tabernacle were holy. Because of God's holiness, his holy place could be dangerous for unqualified people. Moses worked hard to help the people understand and respect the God of Israel. His efforts were becoming successful.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord gave special authority to Aaron, his sons (the priests), and his relatives (the Levites). They were responsible to God for offenses against the holy place. Yet, only the priests were responsible to God for their own violations of God's instructions for their service.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The instructions here came from the need shown in chapter Numbers 17:17 for clear boundaries between the people, priests, and Levites. The Levites had special privileges and important responsibilities. One key part of their job was to protect the Tent of Meeting from unauthorized entry (chapter Numbers 16:16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• all the duties: See Numbers 1:47–53; Numbers 3:5–38; Numbers 4:1–33. 

• they must not come near: The Levites could approach only after they had covered the holy objects for transport.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Aaron and the priests represented the people in the presence of the Lord. Their actions affected all of Israel (see Numbers 16:18–21).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Only the priests, who were Aaron and his descendants, could perform holy duties inside the sanctuary or approach the altar. This altar was a holy area that deserved special honor. Only the high priest could serve in the Most Holy Place. The Levites could only serve in the courtyard, away from the altar. The exception was when it was time to assemble or disassemble the Tent of Meeting (chapter Numbers 4:4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Levites … as a gift to you: Numbers 3–4 explains this phrase. See also Numbers 3:9; Numbers 8:16, Numbers 8:19.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: any outsider … must be put to death: This verse warned all Israelites to avoid areas where God did not allow them to be. God prohibited access to certain holy places for those not qualified in a religious sense. Only the holiest members of the community could access these holy areas. Ignoring this rule meant risking one's life because it violated God's holiness (see also Numbers 1:51, Numbers 1:53; Numbers 3:10, Numbers 3:29–38; Numbers 4:1–20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The priests and Levites received support through the sacrificial system (see, for example, Leviticus 7:28–36). God's chosen representatives deserve payment for their work (compare Matthew 10:9–10; 1 Corinthians 9:3–10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Only Aaron and his sons, the priests set apart to serve in God's presence, consumed the most holy offerings (Exodus 28:1; Exodus 29:44–46). 

• This portion was a holy offering given to God, and the priests had to treat it with respect (Numbers 18:10). Other types of offerings provided food for the priests and their families, but only if they were ceremonially clean (Numbers 18:11–12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Offerings set apart for the Lord were available to Aaron and his extended family. The Hebrew term here means a thing or person totally set apart to the Lord. This could involve either destroying or giving the person of thing as an offering. This verse speaks of an offering (see Leviticus 27:28–29).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord supported the Hebrew priests and their families from the offerings set aside for him. The priests received firstborn animal offerings and the redemption fee for Israel’s firstborn sons. People had to redeem both firstborn sons and the offspring of unclean animals with a silver fee, since they could not sacrifice either one (see Numbers 3:13, Numbers 3:40–51; Exodus 13:2).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: a covenant of salt: These arrangements were part of an eternal and unbreakable covenant (see 2 Chronicles 13:5). The agreement was meant to be permanent because salt, a preservative, symbolized permanence (Leviticus 2:13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The priests and Levites did not have a tribal homeland. They lived scattered among Israel's other tribes (see Numbers 35:1–8; Deuteronomy 12:12; Joshua 21:1–42). 

• I am your portion and your inheritance: Instead of land, Israel's priests had assurance that God himself would be their homeland. The tribe of Levi received tithes as payment for their holy service.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites gave a tithe, which was one-tenth of their yearly income (see Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 26:12; Nehemiah 10:35–39; Malachi 3:8–12; Matthew 23:23; compare Genesis 14:17–20; Hebrews 7:5–10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Levites received a tithe (one-tenth) of the goods of the Israelites (Numbers 18:24). However, they were not allowed to keep all of it. They also had to give a tithe of that tithe, which means one-tenth of the one-tenth. They gave this portion to the priests as their own harvest offering (Numbers 18:27).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Levites and their families could eat any food received as tithes. This food was their payment for working at the Tent of Meeting.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The food tithes were holy gifts from the people of Israel. They could not use these gifts for something common by failing to give a portion to the priests.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: They made the water for the purification ceremony with ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:9). It might be the same as the water of purification in Numbers 8:7 (see also Numbers 31:19–24). This ceremony needed the ashes of a red heifer. The color probably represented blood (compare Hebrews 9:13–14).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This section explains how ordinary Israelites can become ceremonially clean again after touching a corpse and avoid defiling the Tent of Meeting (see Numbers 9:4–12; Leviticus 17:15; Leviticus 21:1–4, Leviticus 21:11–12). God's holiness demands that the place of his presence remains pure and separate from pollution (compare 1 Corinthians 6:9–11, 1 Corinthians 6:18–20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: To protect Aaron’s holy status, Eleazar had to perform the red heifer offering because it caused ceremonial impurity (see Leviticus 21:10–12). The red heifer ceremony differed from the regular sacrifice (compare Leviticus 4:3–12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The only other passage where cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool appear together is Leviticus 14. That chapter describes another ceremony (also "outside the camp") that resulted in ceremonial purification.

Some scholars suggest Eleazar added cedar wood and hyssop for their aroma. Hyssop is associated with purification (Exodus 12:22; Psalm 51:7; compare Hebrews 9:19). The scarlet yarn, like the red heifer, probably symbolizes blood. Together, the cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool symbolize cleansing.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: It required three people to produce and collect the heifer’s ashes. These were Eleazar, the person who burned the animal, and the person who gathered its ashes. All three became ceremonially impure for a day because of this process. The same was true for the person who used the finished product. This was a potion made from the ash dust and water (compare Numbers 19:21). This potion had the same defiling effect as blood associated with sacrifices (Leviticus 6:27–28).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The ceremony of burning the red heifer intended to produce ashes. They collected these ashes and stored them in a pure place outside the camp. The Israelites used them in water for purification ceremonies to remove pollution, such as contact with a corpse (Numbers 19:11–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
If someone touched a human dead body, that person became ceremonially unclean for seven days (compare Leviticus 21:1–3). This meant a person was not allowed to take part in worship until they were made clean. 

To become clean again, the person had to use the water of purification. This water was sprinkled on the third day and again on the seventh day.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Becoming unclean by touching a dead body was very serious. A person who was ceremonially defiled (not fit for worship) could also make the Lord’s tabernacle unclean (compare Leviticus 15:31). 

Because of this danger, such impurity could lead to being “cut off” from the community of Israel. This meant being removed from the people, and in some cases, it could mean death (see Numbers 9:13; Exodus 12:15; Leviticus 7:20–21; Leviticus 17:4–14; Leviticus 20:17–18).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Death made a person ceremonially unclean, and this uncleanness could spread. It could pass to an object or to a place where someone had died (compare Leviticus 15:1–12). This means that anything connected to the dead body could also become unclean. People had to be careful so that impurity did not spread through the camp.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: To cleanse with the heifer's ashes, they made a special purifying mixture. They combined ashes from the burnt purification offering with fresh water (compare Numbers 5:17).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Everyone in Miriam's generation also died (Numbers 14:26–30). This included Moses and Aaron (Numbers 20:2–13, Numbers 20:22–29).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: there was no water: Most of the year, Sinai and the Negev are very hot and dry.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The people of Israel complained again about not having water and food (compare Numbers 11:4–35; Numbers 21:4–5; Exodus 15:22–25). So, Moses and Aaron disobeyed the Lord. As a result, they lost the privilege of entering the promised land.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
our brothers: This shows that the Israelites saw themselves as connected to those who had died:

• Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1–5),

• those who died during the first plague after craving meat (Numbers 11:33),

• the skeptics who died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29),

• the ten unfaithful spies (Numbers 14:36–37),

• Korah, Abiram, and Dathan (Numbers 16:32),

• the 250 leaders (Numbers 16:35), and

• the 14,700 people who died in the second plague (Numbers 16:49).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: They fell facedown: As in earlier conflicts, they lay down and waited for the Lord's glorious presence to resolve the crisis (Numbers 14:5, Numbers 14:10; Numbers 16:4, Numbers 16:19, Numbers 16:22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
God heard Israel’s complaints and accepted them as valid. He did not ignore their concerns.

Then God told Moses to deal with the problem and provide a solution.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses placed the staff in front of the ark of the covenant to stop the Israelites from complaining (compare Numbers 17:10). The staff represented God's authority given to Moses and Aaron. God's instructions to his representatives are very precise and require exact obedience (compare James 3:1; also see 2 Timothy 2:24–26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Instead of obeying God's instructions with respect, Moses criticized the people (Must we bring you water out of this rock?). Moses then hit the rock twice with his staff (Numbers 20:11). God considered the words and actions of Moses as a serious lack of faith. Moses "spoke rashly" (Psalm 106:32–33; compare James 1:20). Moses did not trust God enough to show God’s holiness to the people.

God had told Moses exactly what to do. By acting differently, Moses showed a lack of faith that God would provide for his people. His angry words also revealed this lack of trust.

The Lord requires obedience and faith. Anything less dishonors his holy character (Numbers 20:24; Numbers 27:14). Such a serious lack of obedience and faith led to the same outcome as earlier (Numbers 14:20–23; see also 1 Corinthians 10:4–12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Meribah means “Arguing” or “Quarreling.” As they had earlier at Rephidim(Exodus 17:1–7), the Israelites gave a name that described what happened there. The name pointed more to the event than to the place itself. 

• At Meribah, God showed his holiness through judgment. He disciplined both Aaron and Moses for their sin.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Israel tried to make peace with Edom, but they did not succeed. The two nations had not had contact since the time when Esau (also called Edom) and Jacob (also called Israel) buried their father Isaac(Genesis 35:29; Genesis 36:6–8; see also Genesis 32:28). 

Moses sent a formal message to the king of Edom. His request followed the style of official letters used in that time. While Israel often fought with the Canaanites and other groups, they spoke politely to Edom because the two peoples were related (see also Deuteronomy 2:4; Deuteronomy 23:7). 

Even so, family ties were not strong enough to remove the old tension between Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27:41).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites started their journey to the promised land here. They moved from Kadesh, leaving the Sinai peninsula. They entered the area east of the Jordan River, known as Transjordan. They approached the promised land from the east, taking a less direct route (see Numbers 14:25; compare Deuteronomy 2:2–6).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• We will not … drink water from any well: Edom was a very dry land. Food and water were limited, and there was not enough to support such a large group of Hebrew travelers.

• We will stay on the King’s Highway: This road is mentioned several times in the Old Testament, but its exact path is not fully known (also Numbers 21:22). It was an official road used for government business, trade, and the movement of armies.

Along this road, travelers could find towns, food, and water between the Red Sea and Damascus. The road remained important during Roman times and even later. It was different from another route farther east called the Desert Highway, which was much harder and less welcoming for travelers.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: You may not travel through our land: Just as their ancestor Esau did not trust Jacob, the Edomites now did not trust Jacob’s descendants (Genesis 27:36). Therefore, Israel had to turn around and find another way to approach Canaan (compare Deuteronomy 2:4–6).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Israel did not take the shorter route through the southern area east of the Jordan River. That region was the main territory of Edom (Numbers 20:21). 

• After they left Kadesh, the Hebrews came to Mount Hor. This mountain stood on the border of Edom. The exact location of Mount Hor is not known today. However, the Jewish historian Josephus, who wrote between AD 70 and AD 100, connected it with the region of Petra. He identified it with Jebel Haroun, which means “mountain of Aaron.”

entries.title: Numbers
