entries.content: Aaron’s participation in the rebellion of his generation resulted in his death outside the promised land (Numbers 20:10–12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Moses transferred priestly authority to Eleazar by giving him Aaron's priestly garments (compare Leviticus 8:7–9). After this, Aaron died at 123 years old, in the fortieth year after the Hebrews left Egypt (see Numbers 33:37–39). 

• the entire house of Israel mourned for him thirty days: This was a great honor (see also Deuteronomy 34:8). The usual public mourning period was seven days (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• the Canaanite king of Arad: It is possible that the Canaanite king of Arad felt threatened by many enemies south of his territory (compare Numbers 14:44–45). This may explain why he attacked Israel.

• Arad and Hormah (Numbers 21:3) were far north of Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22–29; Numbers 21:4; see study note on 20:22–23). Ancient Arad is usually identified with Tell Arad. It is west of the modern Israeli town of Arad and about 80 kilometers (50 miles) north of Kadesh. 

Excavations at Tell Arad have found important remains from the Early Bronze Age (about 3300–2000 BC) and the Iron Age (about 1200–500 BC). However, there is no clear evidence that people lived there during the Late Bronze Age (1500–1200 BC), the time of Israel’s exodus and wilderness journey.

Scholars have suggested several explanations:

• Some connect ancient Arad with a different site in the same region. 

• Others argue that these stories were written much later and do not match archaeological discoveries. 

• Still others say the evidence is incomplete and does not allow a final answer.

Similar questions about geography and archaeology appear in other parts of the Old Testament. In many cases, the available evidence does not give a certain conclusion.

• Atharim is not known from any other source.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• As Israel journeyed to the promised land, they traveled from Mount Hor to the plains of Moab (Numbers 22:1). The story of Israel's journey emphasizes the Lord's patient plan to lead Israel into Canaan despite their weaknesses. 

• The general direction of their travel is clear. However, the exact path they took is not known today. Many of the places mentioned are difficult to identify.

Archaeological evidence at some sites does not match the time usually connected with the wilderness period. Because of this, there are still serious questions about geography and history in the wilderness journey.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• devote … to destruction: This phrase translates the Hebrew word kharam. This word means to devote something fully to God by destroying it. Israel was told to completely destroy their enemies and their property in certain cases (see Leviticus 27:28–29; Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:17; Joshua 6–7; Joshua 10:1–11:23). 

• This battle also includes wordplay between kharam and Hormah (Hebrew khormah, Numbers 21:3). The similar sounds connect the action of destroying with the name of the place.

The event marks a turning point in Israel’s dealings with the Canaanites. The Canaanites would continue to be strong and dangerous enemies during the time of the conquest.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The "vow to the LORD" (Numbers 21:2–3) and the resulting victory did not stop Israel from criticizing God and Moses. The long journey was a punishment for similar complaints (Numbers 14:26–35).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This entire region has been, and still is, home to very venomous snakes (compare Isaiah 30:6).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Jesus referred to this event when he explained who he is and why he came (John 3:14–15). 

• By the time of King Hezekiah, around 700 BC, the bronze snake had become an object of worship in Jerusalem. The people were burning incense to it, so Hezekiah destroyed it (2 Kings 18:4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The location of Oboth is uncertain.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Israelites traveled along the east side of Edom. 

• Iye-abarim means "ruins of Abarim" or "ruins of the region beyond." It was probably near the northern bank of Zered Brook (compare Deuteronomy 2:13–14). This brook separated ancient Edom from Moab (Deuteronomy 2:8–25).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Israelites traveled east of the Moabite territory, located between the Zered Brook in the south and the Arnon River in the north. The far side of the Arnon River was probably north and east of the main east–west canyon of the Arnon. This huge canyon acted as a natural boundary between Moab and the Amorite territory north of the Arnon (see Numbers 21:26). 

• The Amorites were a group of nomadic (traveling) peoples. During the Middle Bronze Age (about 2000–1500 BC), they conquered areas from Mesopotamia to Canaan. They even ruled important cities such as Babylon (around 1830 BC) and Assur (around 1750 BC).

Amorites living in the hill country of Canaan had frightened Israel’s spies (Deuteronomy 1:26–28). Later, they defeated Israel when the people tried to enter Canaan without God’s command (Numbers 14:44–45; see Deuteronomy 1:42–44). 

When Israel arrived east of the Jordan River, the Amorites controlled much of that region. This area is called Transjordan, which means the land east of the Jordan (see study note on Numbers 21:26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• the Book of the Wars of the LORD: This is similar to The Book of Jashar (Joshua 10:13; 2 Samuel 1:18). The Book of the Wars of the Lord is not known from any other source.

• Waheb, a town, and Suphah, a region, are not known from any other record. Their exact locations are unknown.

Ar was one of the main settlements of Moab at that time (compare Numbers 21:28; Deuteronomy 2:18; Isaiah 15:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The location of Beer is unknown (compare Isaiah 15:8). The short poem in this passage describes the digging of a new well. It shows the joy the people felt. In a dry region, a new source of water was a great blessing.

The poem says that princes and leaders dug the well. It also says they used scepters and staffs, which were symbols of authority. This may suggest that the digging of the well was part of a special or joyful ceremony.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: After moving north of the Arnon, the Hebrews left the wilderness on the eastern side of Moab and the newly conquered Amorite territory (see study note on 21:21–35). They turned west toward the ridgeline that rises up from the Jordan Rift valley, then traveled north to Pisgah Peak (see also Numbers 23:14; Deuteronomy 3:17, Deuteronomy 3:27; Deuteronomy 34:1, Deuteronomy 34:5).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Compare Numbers 20:14–17.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: King Sihon's land was between Moab and Ammon. God would not allow the Israelites to invade Ammon, Edom, or Moab (Deuteronomy 2:19; Deuteronomy 2:4–9). This was because they were relatives (Genesis 19:30–38; Genesis 32:3). Yet, Israel needed to cross Transjordan (the region across the Jordan River) to enter Canaan. Sihon's territory was the natural route.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Israelite victories over King Sihon of Heshbon and King Og of Bashan previewed the Hebrew conquest of Canaan. It came to represent God's promise to help his people when they were in need (see Numbers 13:10–12; Deuteronomy 2:24–3:7; Joshua 2:10; Joshua 9:10; Joshua 12:1–6; Judges 11:19–22; Nehemiah 9:22; Psalms 135:10–12; Psalms 136:17–22; Jeremiah 48:45–46). 

• Israel had left the wilderness before reaching Pisgah (compare Numbers 21:18, Numbers 21:23; Numbers 21:20). So, this story probably indicates an earlier event before the movement in Numbers 21:18–20.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh settled in the area conquered at this time (compare chapter Numbers 32:32).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Sihon king of the Amorites captured the area north of the Arnon from the Moabites, who controlled it earlier. Israel then occupied this region for several hundred years. King Mesha of Moab reclaimed it around 830 BC (see 2 Kings 3:4–27). This came through a campaign detailed on the Mesha Inscription (also known as the Moabite Stone). 

• Heshbon is usually considered to be Tell Hesban. No evidence yet has shown that people lived there in the Late Bronze Age (see study note on Numbers 21:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
This ancient song may have been an old Amorite ballad about the victories of King Sihon. It may have celebrated his power and success.

Other interpreters believe that Israelite singers wrote the song later. In this view, it was a taunt song meant to mock Sihon’s defeat and celebrate Israel’s victory.

The flow of the story from Numbers 21:26 to Numbers 21:27 supports the first view. Israel may have taken an older Amorite song and applied it to their own victory. Sihon and the Amorites had once defeated Moab. Now Israel had defeated them. Compare Judges 11:12–28.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: King Sihon had destroyed Moab’s towns from his center of operations at Heshbon.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: From the ancient point of view, even Moab’s supreme god Chemosh suffered defeat at the hands of the Amorite conquerors, while the people of Moab became refugees and captives.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The area described here is the one Israel had just conquered (Numbers 21:24). The song celebrating Sihon is a fitting tribute to Israel's victory.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Ancient Bashan was east of the Sea of Galilee. 

• King Og, like Sihon, was an Amorite (see study note on 21:13). Deuteronomy 3:1–11 details the story of Israel defeating Og.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: they took possession of his land: See chapter Numbers 32:32.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: After defeating the Amorite kingdoms, Israel settled in the plains of Moab (Numbers 21:21–35 and study note). This area is on the eastern side of the Jordan Valley, northeast of the Dead Sea, and across the river from Jericho's oasis. The Hebrews camped there until they crossed the Jordan River to enter Canaan (Joshua 3:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: There is no mention of Balak outside of this event (Joshua 24:9; Judges 11:25; Micah 6:5; Revelation 2:14). Sihon, the Amorite king, had taken over his territory (Numbers 21:26). Israel had just defeated Sihon (Numbers 21:21–31). Balak might have thought his small kingdom would be next.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The story of Balak and Balaam marks an important turning point in Israel’s history. It includes humor, drama, and deep teaching about God.

The story makes one main point clear. The Lord’s will must be carried out. No one could stop his plan for Israel.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Midian: This desert people descended from Abraham (Genesis 25:1–2; Exodus 2:15–16). Their agreement with Moab started their conflicts with Israel (Numbers 22:7; see Numbers 25:6, Numbers 25:14–18; Numbers 31:2–10; Judges 6–8).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Balaam was a pagan religious specialist called a diviner. A diviner was someone who claimed to receive messages from the spiritual world and predict the future. Balaam came from northwest Mesopotamia (see “Balaam” Profile). 

Like many ancient peoples, the nations of Moab and Midian believed that spoken words had power. They believed that a blessing or a curse spoken by a skilled diviner could shape future events. Diviners claimed they had special power to discover and influence what would happen next (see Deuteronomy 18:14; 1 Samuel 6:2; 2 Kings 21:6; Isaiah 44:25; Daniel 2:1–12, Daniel 2:27–28; Micah 5:12; Zechariah 10:2). 

Israel’s enemies asked Balaam to place curses on the Hebrews. They believed that his spoken words would harm them. In the ancient world, armies often spoke curses against their enemies before battle.

People in ancient Israel also believed that spoken words could have real effect, even when they were not part of divination (for example, Genesis 27:1–40; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; 1 Samuel 14:24–28; compare Matthew 21:18–22). 

• Pethor is probably the ancient city of Pitru (Numbers 22:5). It was located on the west side of the Euphrates River, south of Carchemish, about 640 kilometers (400 miles) from Moab.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: departed with the fees for divination in hand: Balaam was a professional diviner and could demand a high payment for his services (Numbers 22:7, Numbers 22:17–18; compare 1 Samuel 9:7–8; 2 Kings 8:7–9).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Spend the night here: Balaam expected to receive a message from God at night (Numbers 22:9, Numbers 22:19–20; compare Job 4:12–16; Zechariah 1:8). 

• the LORD (Hebrew Yahweh): Balaam knew about Yahweh, the God of Israel, and expected a message from him about what to do.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God commanded Balaam not to go with Balak's messengers.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Some people think Balaam answered the second group of messengers in a way that tried to gain a larger reward. They suggest that he wanted a more profitable offer.

However, Balaam later said that he could not go beyond the command of the Lord, even for a great reward (Numbers 24:13). This statement makes that view less likely.

Instead, Balaam appeared determined to obey the Lord. He even called the Lord “my God,” which shows that he recognized the Lord’s authority.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balaam agreed to ask about the Lord's wishes once more. God allowed him to go with Balak’s representatives but warned him to follow God's commands exactly (see Numbers 22:35).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This passage clearly uses humor to make fun of Balaam, the professional diviner. The story shows that his spiritual understanding and obedience to God were less than those of his own donkey.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
God’s anger may seem surprising because he had given Balaam permission to go in Numbers 22:20. However, the Lord knew that Balaam’s true motives were not as honest as he claimed when he spoke with Balak’s messengers.

Balaam’s harsh beating of his donkey reveals a lack of godly character (Proverbs 12:10; compare 1 Samuel 25:1 Samuel 25).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The only similar event in Scripture is the serpent talking to Eve (Genesis 3:1–5). God used the donkey to correct the foolish diviner (2 Peter 2:15–16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
I have sinned: Balaam admitted he was wrong. He realized that he had not seen the angel of the Lord standing in his way. He also had not understood the angel’s purpose.

Balaam offered to turn back and not continue on the journey.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord ensured that Balaam would say only what God commanded (compare Numbers 22:20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: It is likely that this meeting place was in the northeastern corner of Balak’s small kingdom.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balak thought Balaam did not understand how urgent the situation was nor how great the offered payment.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balaam’s answer showed that he had learned from what happened with the donkey (compare Numbers 22:20, Numbers 22:35).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Balak tried to get Balaam to curse Israel. First, he used a ceremonial offering and meal to summon the gods and Balaam. Then, he took Balaam to view the Israelite camp. 

• Kiriath-huzoth is an unknown location.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Bamoth-baal means "high places of Baal." It was on a ridge of hills above the plains of Moab, northeast of the Dead Sea (compare "Bamoth" in Numbers 21:19; Joshua 13:17). It was the first of three places where the Moabite king took Balaam to view the large, spread-out Israelite camp (also Numbers 22:41; Numbers 23:14, Numbers 23:28). From this high point, he could see the Israelites and perform ceremonies (Numbers 22:11). Balak hoped these would result in a strong curse against them.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The number seven was a holy symbol (also Numbers 23:4, Numbers 23:14, Numbers 23:29; compare Job 42:8; see “Symbolic Numbers” Theme Note).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• As a diviner, Balaam carried out rituals to look for signs about the future of Israel (compare Numbers 23:23; Numbers 24:1). Balak had called him to curse Israel, but God repeatedly stopped him. 

• These sacrifices might have related to extispicy. This was the practice of examining animal livers or other organs to predict the future. Ancient Near Eastern texts show that this fortune-telling method was common and well-developed. God had forbidden Israel from such practices (see Deuteronomy 18:9–14; compare Ezekiel 21:21).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Instead of cursing Israel, Balaam spoke about their special status (compare Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6–9). He recognized that God's blessing had transformed a humble people into a great nation (compare Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 13:16; Genesis 28:14). Balaam hoped for similar good fortune for himself (Numbers 23:10).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• In his first message from God, Balaam reviewed why he had come to Moab (Numbers 23:5, Numbers 23:16). He explained how Balak had called him. He also stressed that God had a special relationship with Israel. Balaam made clear that he could not harm Israel because God was protecting them.

• These messages are written as poetry. Hebrew poetry often uses parallelism. Parallelism places two similar lines together. The second line repeats or strengthens the first line in a clear and ordered way.

• Aram: This refers to Aram-naharaim. This name describes North Mesopotamia, where Balaam’s hometown of Pethor was located (Numbers 22:5). 

• the mountains of the east: This refers to a mountain range in North Syria.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balak hoped for different results by changing the location. The exact location of the plateau of Zophim on Pisgah Peak is unknown. Yet, Pisgah is part of the ridge that is above the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 34:1). It is near Bamoth-baal and Mount Peor (Numbers 22:41; Numbers 23:28).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
This message emphasizes God’s faithfulness to his people. He would remain with them and keep all the promises he had made.

Nothing would cause him to abandon his word or turn away from Israel.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Because God is faithful and always keeps his word, Balaam had no choice but to bless Israel.

He could not speak against them because God had decided to bless them.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord kept his promises to bless his people, bringing them no misfortune or trouble. Balaam could not change God's plans. God punished the Hebrews for disobedience. Yet, he supported Israel's cause ever since he freed them from Egypt.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: No curse could overpower Israel because God blessed them (Numbers 22:12; compare Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 22:17–18). Israel was safe from the harm that Moab and Midian tried to cause through divination (compare Numbers 24:1). Israel would become famous because God protected them from harm (see Joshua 2:9–11; compare Numbers 14:13–19).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Unhappy with Balaam's blessing, Balak hoped a new location would change the outcome. Although the exact location of Mount Peor is unknown, it was probably near a worship site for Baal of Peor and the Beth-peor (compare Numbers 25:3, Numbers 25:5). See Deuteronomy 3:29; Deuteronomy 34:6 for where they buried Moses.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Unlike before, Balaam did not use divination this time (Numbers 23:3, Numbers 23:15). He already knew that signs and omens could not harm Israel (Numbers 23:23). So he stopped looking for them. 

Instead, the Spirit of God came directly upon Balaam. God himself gave Balaam the message to speak.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The third message describes God's plan to bless Israel again.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: God showed his love for his people by giving them many blessings. These blessings were signs of his care and favor toward Israel.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Lord’s favor is shown by comparing Israel to groves and gardens that have plenty of water. In a dry land, water brings life and growth. This picture shows how God was caring for his people.

Israel’s growing population also showed God’s blessing (Numbers 24:7; as mentioned in Numbers 23:10). This growth would become even clearer in the second census recorded in chapter Numbers 26:26.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• God's blessing would allow the Israelites defeat their enemies (see Numbers 24:15–24).

• Agag was an Amalekite king whom King Saul defeated (1 Samuel 15:7–9, 1 Samuel 15:32–33). The Amalekites, a desert people, were traditional enemies of the Hebrews (compare Numbers 14:45; Exodus 17:8–16). Agag was probably a traditional title for their king. Since God brought Israel out of Egypt, he fought for them like a warrior and a wild animal (wild ox and lion; Numbers 24:8–9). 

• Blessed … cursed: See Genesis 12:3; Genesis 27:29.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balak clapped his hands to show anger and disapproval (see also Job 27:23; Lamentations 2:15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: come, let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come: Since Balak tried to curse Israel, God would curse him and his people (Numbers 24:9). The harm Balak wanted to cause Israel will instead happen to Moab.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This prophecy gives more specific details than the first three messages. It is based on another vision from God (the Most High, Numbers 24:16). It also predicts the appearance of a great leader who will play a major role in these military victories (Numbers 24:17).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• A star symbolized a king (see Isaiah 14:12; Matthew 2:1–10). A scepter symbolized power and majesty (see Genesis 49:10; Psalm 45:6). 

Historically, King David fits this description. The Moabites, whose defeat Numbers 24:17 mentions, were among the many peoples he conquered during David's rule (2 Samuel 8:2). Yet, Moab remained a threat to Israel after David's time (see 2 Kings 3:1–27; Isaiah 15–16; Jeremiah 48). 

Many interpreters have extended this image beyond David. Christians identify Jesus of Nazareth with a star and a scepter (compare Matthew 2:2; 2 Peter 1:19; Revelation 2:28; Revelation 22:16; compare Hebrews 1:8). 

• the sons of Sheth: These people were probably the ancient Sutu, a group known from other records. 

However, the name may refer to a different people group. It could refer to:

• Edom, also called Seir, which David later defeated (Numbers 24:18),

• Ir, or Ar, a city of Moab (Numbers 24:19; compare Numbers 21:28), or

• Amalek, one of Israel’s earliest and most lasting enemies (Numbers 24:20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Assyria would destroy the Kenites, a desert people living in the same areas as the Amalekites and Midianites. Moses married a Kenite (Judges 1:16; Judges 4:11; compare Numbers 10:29–32). The Kenites were mostly friendly with Israel after that time (for example, 1 Samuel 15:6; 1 Samuel 27:10; 1 Samuel 30:27–30).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: This verse is similar to Numbers 22:12 and summarizes the lesson of the entire event.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The message concludes by mentioning the appearance and downfall of invaders from Cyprus. The Hebrew term Kittim probably referred to various Mediterranean groups (compare Genesis 10:4; Jeremiah 2:10; Daniel 11:30).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Eber has the same spelling as the ancestor of the Hebrews (compare Genesis 10:21–25; Genesis 11:10–16). It may refer to a people on the other side of the Euphrates River. This region fits the parallel reference to Assyria (see Joshua 24:3; Isaiah 7:20).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balaam did not yet go back to Pethor (Numbers 31:8).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• in Shittim: From here, Joshua later sent spies across the Jordan River, and the Hebrews began their conquest (Joshua 2:1; Joshua 3:1). 

• daughters of Moab: The Moabites and the Midianites both shared responsibility for what happened with Balaam (Numbers 22:2–4, Numbers 22:7; Numbers 31:8, Numbers 31:15–16).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Israel was camped across the Jordan River from Jericho. They were almost ready to enter the land and begin the conquest. However, at this important moment, they fell into serious sin.

Balaam advised Israel’s enemies to lead the people into sexual immorality and idolatry at Baal-peor (Numbers 31:16). 

He could not harm Israel with a curse, so he chose another way. He led them into sin through lust and the worship of false gods.

The early church faced similar temptations. Believers were warned about idolatry and sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 10:6, 1 Corinthians 10:11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites participated in worship feasts associated with the gods of Moab (see Psalm 106:28).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Baal of Peor might refer to Chemosh by another name (Numbers 21:29). More likely, it refers to Baal, which means “lord.” Baal was a Canaanite god. The Moabites honored several gods, and Baal was probably one of them.

Many place names include the name Baal, such as Baal-gad, Baal-hermon, Baal-meon, and Baal-peor. These names likely marked local shrines where people worshiped Baal in different forms.

Peor was a mountain from which Balaam could see the camp of Israel in the plains of Moab. Nearby was a shrine called Beth-peor (Numbers 23:28; Numbers 25:3, Numbers 25:5, Numbers 25:18; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 3:29; Deuteronomy 4:3, Deuteronomy 4:46; Deuteronomy 34:6; Joshua 13:20; Joshua 22:17).

• Israel’s worship of false gods made the Lord very angry. As a result, a plague broke out among the people (Numbers 25:8–9; Numbers 26:1; compare Numbers 11:1, Numbers 11:10; Numbers 12:9).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• As at Sinai, the Lord required quick justice (Exodus 32:27–28). 

• execute them in broad daylight: They may have killed the guilty people and hung them on a pole. Then they would leave them in the sun so everyone could see and learn from their mistakes (see 2 Samuel 21:6, 2 Samuel 21:9; compare 2 Samuel 12:12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• In this event, another Israelite man made himself unclean by being with a foreign woman. Both Moabite and Midianite women were involved in this scandal (Numbers 25:1–3, Numbers 25:16–18; Numbers 31:1–2). 

His sin was especially bold. He acted without shame, even though people around him were mourning because of God’s judgment.

• Some interpreters suggest that his tent may have been more than his personal dwelling. They think it may have been an unauthorized shrine connected with the worship of Yahweh. If so, this would have made his sin even more serious.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Phinehas, acting as a representative of the priestly family, killed Zimri and Cozbi with one thrust of a spear (Numbers 25:7–8). The text likely suggests that they were engaged in sexual relations at that moment.

Phinehas acted with zeal, which means strong passion to defend God’s honor. His action brought the plague to an end (Numbers 25:1–3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Israel’s identity as the Lord’s people was in great danger because they were unfaithful at this time. Their sin threatened their special relationship with God.

Phinehas showed strong zeal (deep commitment and passion) for God’s holiness and justice. He acted in a way that matched God’s own concern for what is right. Because of this, God gave Phinehas and his descendants a special blessing.

God made a covenant of peace (a lasting promise of peace and favor) with Phinehas. The men in his family who were qualified could serve as priests forever (compare Malachi 2:5). 

This covenant was unconditional (it did not depend on future actions). It was similar to the covenant God made with David (see Jeremiah 33:19–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The deaths of Zimri and Cozbi helped remove sin from the community of Israel. Their judgment stopped the spread of sin among the people.

Phinehas’s action had atoning value. This means it helped turn away God’s judgment and restore the people’s relationship with him. His act brought cleansing and peace to Israel (see study note on Leviticus 1:4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Attack the Midianites and strike them dead: This war is recorded in chapter Numbers 31:31.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
As in the first census, Moses and Eleazar directed the counting of the people. Eleazar had taken Aaron’s place as high priest.

They gave instructions to the tribal leaders about how to record the numbers of the men.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: After nearly 40 years, Israel registered their men of military age again. This was while camping on the plains of Moab across from Jericho (compare chapters Numbers 1:1–4). The overall population changed only slightly, with 603,550 in the first registration and 601,730 in the second. This nearly complete replacement of the population showed that the Lord remained faithful to Israel despite their repeated acts of rebellion (Numbers 26:63–65).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the line of Korah did not die out: See study note on 16:31–33 for more information.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The daughters of Zelophehad began an important change in Israel’s law (see Numbers 27:1–11; Numbers 36:1–12).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Despite wars, plagues, and punishments, God remained faithful to Israel. The number of male warriors decreased by 1,820 compared to the first count. This was a difference of 0.3 percent (compare Numbers 2:32).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The second registration, like the first, was for military purposes. It also helped distribute land to Israel's tribes based on their populations (see Joshua 15–19). 

• the land must be divided by lot: People used lots to seek guidance from God and prevent favoritism in important matters (for example, Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 10:20; 1 Samuel 14:41–42; Proverbs 18:18; Acts 1:26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The family of Kohath received special attention as the clan of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Moses counted the Levites separately (compare Numbers 1:47–49; Numbers 3:14–39). 

• a month old or more: Compare Numbers 3:15. 

• The Levites did not receive a land allotment when the Israelites divided the land. Instead, they received 48 towns for their use, but no large territory as described in Numbers 26:52–56. (Numbers 35:1–8; compare Numbers 18:23–24).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The numbers in this second registration describe a completely new generation of Hebrews. Everyone who had left Egypt had died in the wilderness except Caleb and Joshua.

Joshua became the leader of Israel after Moses (Numbers 27:12–23; see “Joshua” Profile). Caleb also later played an important role in Israel’s history (see “Caleb” Profile). 

Numbers 26 shows an important change. The earlier generation had lived under God’s judgment because of their unbelief (chapter Numbers 14:14). Now a new generation stood ready for the future, just as Balaam’s four prophecies had promised (chapters Numbers 23:23–24).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Zelophehad did not have any sons, which allowed for changes to the inheritance laws. They would later refine these laws more (compare Numbers 36:1–13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the entrance of the Tent of Meeting: This was the most important public place, where leaders made important decisions. Joshua 17:4 specifically mentions Eleazar, Joshua, and the Hebrew leaders. But it does not mention Moses. These women asked for an exception to the existing law and presented their case to the highest tribal authorities.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Zelophehad had not joined Korah’s rebellion (Numbers 16:1–50).If he had taken part in that rebellion, he may have lost his property rights because of his sin (see Numbers 15:30; compare 1 Kings 21:7–16). 

Israelite society was patriarchal and patrilineal. This means that family ancestry and property were passed down through the male line. Normally, sons inherited their father’s land.

Zelophehad had no sons. His daughters wanted their father’s land to remain in their family. They asked for property rights equal to those given to sons. Their request was reasonable and based on a desire to preserve their family’s inheritance.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Moses brought their case before the Lord. The Lord accepted the women’s request.

God then established their case as a general rule. This new rule helped preserve property within families when there were no sons to inherit it.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: this mountan of the Abarim range: This was probably Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 32:49). From this mountain, Moses looked over the promised land shortly before he died (Deuteronomy 34:1).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel needed a leader when they entered the land of Canaan. Joshua was chosen to follow Moses.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel was about to begin a long battle for Canaan. Moses did not want them to struggle without a leader or become lost like sheep without a shepherd (compare 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Matthew 9:36).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Joshua was well prepared to become Israel’s leader. He had already led Israel in battle (compare Exodus 17:8–16). He had also served as Moses’s assistant for many years (Numbers 11:28; compare Exodus 33:11). 

Joshua was one of the two faithful spies who knew the people of Israel well (Numbers 13–14). The Spirit of God was with Joshua (compare Numbers 11:25–29). His close relationship with God gave him wisdom for the work ahead (for example, Deuteronomy 34:9). 

• lay your hands on him: This act symbolized transferring authority from an elder leader to his assistant (compare Numbers 8:10–14). Moses did this publicly so that no one would question Joshua's leadership.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Joshua received only part of the authority Moses had. Moses had spoken with God face to face (Numbers 12:6–8; Deuteronomy 34:10–12). Joshua did not have that same direct access to God’s revelation.

Instead, Joshua had to seek guidance through Eleazar the priest on important matters (Numbers 27:21; compare Exodus 28:30; Leviticus 8:8). Eleazar used the priestly means of seeking God’s will.

From this time on, Israel separated military leadership from spiritual leadership. Joshua led the army, while the priest guided the people in spiritual matters.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord accepted special gifts as a pleasing aroma (compare Numbers 15:3). This means God accepted and enjoyed these gifts (see also Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18). The priests made offerings at set times following specific instructions (see Numbers 28:3–29:39).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• These two chapters describe Israel's ceremonial calendar. It listed daily, weekly, and monthly offerings, along with annual religious events. God instructed Israel to worship him "in a proper and orderly manner" (1 Corinthians 14:40). 

The annual sacrifices required many animals, grain, oil, and wine. On these special days, Israel stopped their usual work. This was a sacrifice that emphasized the importance of these holy days. 

The annual cycle included eight different occasions for worship, each reflecting Israel's relationship with the Lord. Each event involved different combinations of burnt, grain, liquid, or sin offerings. 

• For details on grain and liquid offerings, see Numbers 15:1–16. For explanations of different offerings, see Leviticus 1:1–7:38. For a description of Israel's festivals, see Leviticus 23:1–44. For the New Testament view on the Old Testament sacrificial system, see John 1:29; Romans 12:1; Hebrews 9:9–15; Hebrews 10:1–2; 1 Peter 2:5.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the food: See study notes on Exodus 29:18 and Deuteronomy 8:2.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The daily offering was the foundation of the sacrificial system. This practice began at Mount Sinai (see Exodus 29:38–46). 

• fermented drink: Compare Numbers 6:3; Leviticus 10:9; Deuteronomy 14:26.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Special days required extra offerings. On the Sabbath, people made a sacrifice in addition to the regular burnt offering and its liquid offering. Other passages emphasize the importance of the Sabbath (for example, Exodus 20:8–11; Leviticus 23:3; Deuteronomy 5:12–15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The first day of each month was the new moon. On that day, the people sacrificed bulls, rams, and lambs as burnt offerings. They also sacrificed a male goat as a sin offering (an offering for forgiveness of sin).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Passover, followed by the Feast of Unleavened Bread, was the first of five major annual feasts. It took place in early spring (March or April). The Passover did not require public sacrifices. It was a family event celebrated at home (see also Numbers 9:1–4; Exodus 12:1–13:10; Leviticus 23:5–8; Deuteronomy 16:1–8). 

This festival is important in the background of the Last Supper (see Matthew 26:17–19, Matthew 26:26–27; Mark 14:12; John 11:55; John 12:1; John 13:1; John 18:28, John 18:39; John 19:14, John 19:31; compare 1 Corinthians 5:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Feast of Weeks was later called the Feast of Pentecost (see Acts 2:1; also Leviticus 23:15–22). It marked the end of the barley harvest and the start of the wheat harvest in early summer (May or June). The Greek name Pentecost means “fiftieth.” It refers to the fiftieth day after Passover (see Acts 20:16; 1 Corinthians 16:8).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: a day for you to sound the trumpets: See also Leviticus 23:23–25.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: On the tenth day of this seventh month: Today this day is known as Yom Kippur. The name comes from the Hebrew yom hakkippurim, which means “day of atonement” (a day for seeking forgiveness for sin, Leviticus 23:27).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Day of Atonement was a serious and holy day. It was a day of fasting, when the people did not eat food as a sign of repentance and prayer (see also Leviticus 16; Leviticus 23:26–32; Romans 3:23–25; Hebrews 9:7–12, Hebrews 9:23–28).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Feast of Tabernacles began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. It was an eight-day harvest celebration that required many offerings (Numbers 29:12, Numbers 29:35; Exodus 34:22). This festival was a joyful time for giving thanks (see Nehemiah 8:13–18). The tabernacles (or shelters) reminded the Israelites of living in tents during their time in the wilderness (see also Leviticus 23:33–43; 1 Kings 8:1–2).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The public offerings were not the only sacrifices. People also brought their own voluntary gifts (see Leviticus 23:38).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Vows included promises to give offerings, like Hannah's vow in 1 Samuel 1:1 Samuel 1. It included pledges to abstain from certain things, like the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6. Jesus mentioned the teachings about vows in the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5:33.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Vows were an important way to show devotion or piety. But people sometimes made them quickly and forgot them. People often made voluntary pledges during special religious events or in times of war. The mention of vows and voluntary offerings might have led to further discussion here (Numbers 29:39; compare Numbers 15:3; see also Numbers 6:1–21; Leviticus 5:4–5; Leviticus 27:1–34; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). 

These instructions applied to Hannah and Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:1–28). Such practices, including fasting, continued into the New Testament period (for example, Matthew 6:16; Matthew 15:3–9; Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23). Vows made by females needed approval from the responsible male who would share financial responsibility for the vow. This applied to young and unmarried or adult and married women. No one, male or female, young or old, should make a vow to God and then ignore it.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: A young woman was under her father's authority. He was responsible for her actions and financial obligations.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: When a young Hebrew woman married, her husband gained authority over her. He could cancel any vow or pledge she made while under her father's authority. This was only true if he canceled it as soon as he heard about it.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: A widow or divorced woman usually returned to her father's family (Leviticus 22:13). Yet, a mature single woman who made a vow or pledge had to fulfill her religious duties.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
A married woman needed her husband's approval to make vows and pledges. Her husband could cancel her religious promise. But he had to decide on the day he heard about it. God did not blame the married woman for breaking the promise if her husband canceled it correctly (compare Numbers 30:5, Numbers 30:8, Numbers 30:12). 

The self-denial mentioned in Numbers 30:13 probably refers to fasting. If he did not object, the husband's silence meant he agreed. He could not delay his objection, or he would be guilty of a broken vow (compare Leviticus 5:4–13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Lord instructed Moses to lead Israel in a war against the Midianites. The Midianites had joined the Moabites in influencing the Hebrews to worship idols (chapter Numbers 25:25). The Midianites were a tribal people living in the dry regions south and east of Palestine and east of the Jordan River. They were among the "people of the east" (Judges 6:3, Judges 6:33; Judges 7:12). They lived in camps or settlements and were famous for their desert transportation skills (compare Genesis 37:28, Genesis 37:36; Isaiah 60:6). 

They descended from Abraham and had been friendly to Moses (Genesis 25:1–2; Exodus 2:15–3:1; compare Numbers 10:29). Yet, the elders of Midian joined Balak in hiring Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22:4, Numbers 22:7). Israel's presence threatened the peoples of Transjordan (the area east of the Jordan River).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Each tribe sent 1,000 men to the battle. This allowed everyone to gain combat experience and share the victory.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Phinehas, son of Eleazar the high priest, led this force of 12,000 men into battle. His leadership showed that this battle was considered a “holy war” (a war carried out in obedience to God). It was an act of judgment for the spiritual harm that Midian had caused Israel (see Numbers 25:6–18; Numbers 31:15–16). His zeal in this situation matched his actions in the case of Zimri and Cozbi (Numbers 25:11, Numbers 25:13; Numbers 25:7–8). 

• Many scholars believe the holy objects of the holy place included the ark of the covenant, which the Hebrews sometimes carried into battle (for example, Numbers 10:35–36; Joshua 6:6; 1 Samuel 4:3–11; see also Numbers 14:44). Other scholars suggest they were various holy objects used in Tent of Meeting ceremonies (Numbers 3:31; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 18:3; see also 1 Kings 8:4; 1 Chronicles 9:29; 2 Chronicles 5:5). The Israelites likely took some or all of these holy objects as signs that God was with them in this battle.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Israelites killed all of the Midianite men in the particular groups they attacked from their camp in the plains of Moab (Numbers 31:12). They did not destroy all the Midianites who were part of the larger Midianite alliance (compare Judges 6–8). The number of animals and virgins mentioned in Numbers 31:32–35 shows that the 12,000 Hebrews fought a large enemy army.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Balaam son of Beor was put to death because his advice caused the people of Israel to turn against the Lord at Mount Peor (Numbers 31:16). He was judged for his evil actions (compare 2 Peter 2:15; Jude 1:11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: After the battle, the Hebrews began the practice that they sometimes followed throughout the period of conquest and beyond (for example, Joshua 6; Joshua 8:8; Joshua 10:10–11). They destroyed their enemies (sometimes the total population), burned towns, and set aside spoils for their own use or as dedicated to the Lord.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: cities … encampments: These places included both large towns and smaller camps without walls.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: outside the camp: The returning troops probably observed ceremonies to make themselves ceremonially clean. This was to avoid making the Tent of Meeting and the people unclean through contact with dead bodies (Numbers 31:19–24).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses was angry: God had commanded the Israelites to destroy everything. But the Midianite women who had followed Balaam’s advice were allowed to live. These women had played a major role in leading Israel into sin at Baal Peor.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Only young, virgin women were to be spared. They were allowed to live because they had not taken part in the sin at Baal Peor.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Israelite soldiers who touched dead bodies became ceremonially unclean (ritually impure). They had to go through the required purification rituals.

These rituals were routine, but they were important. They also had to purify their equipment (see Numbers 5:1–4; Numbers 19:1–22).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: They divided the plunder into two equal parts. Half went to those who fought against the Midianites and half to the Israelites who stayed behind (compare 1 Samuel 30:21–25). In this way, everyone participated in the conflict. Yet, the smaller group of soldiers each received a larger portion than the much larger group who stayed behind.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The total number of animals and young girls who were not killed was quite large, which shows that Israel fought against many Midianites.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The plunder was distributed according to the principles established in Numbers 31:25–30.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
It is unusual for an army to lose no soldiers in battle, but it is not impossible. Ancient writers also described battles in which few or no Roman soldiers were killed.

If the Israelites were well prepared and attacked by surprise, and if they had many more soldiers than their enemies, they could have won the battle without losing any men. This would be even more likely because of God’s blessing.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The commanders happily offered gold objects to show gratitude for a great victory with no loss of life (see Exodus 30:12). Ancient art and literature show that the Midianites and other desert peoples, both men and women, wore gold jewelry. They used it as decoration, and as a form of wealth they could take with them (for example, Judges 8:24–26). 

Moses and Eleazar brought this large collection to the Tent of Meeting as a memorial of this special event (compare Numbers 16:39–40; Zechariah 6:14).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• very large herds and flocks: The Israelites had flocks and herds when they left Egypt (see Exodus 12:38). They gained more animals as plunder in the war with Midian (see Numbers 31:32–33). They might have also gained it in their victories over Sihon and Og (see Numbers 21:21–35). 

• Gilead can refer to either the entire northern region of the plateau east of the Jordan River (for example, Numbers 32:29). It can also refer only to the land between the Jabbok River and the Arnon River.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
After Israel took control of the central area east of the Jordan River, during the battles described in chapter Numbers 21:21, they began preparing to enter Canaan.

At that time, the Israelites needed to remain united. But two tribes asked for permission to settle on the east side of the Jordan River instead of crossing into Canaan.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled in the land Israel had recently captured from Sihon the Amorite and Og of Bashan (see Numbers 21:21–35). 

• Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, and Elealeh have been connected with known archaeological sites. These places have been identified with ruins that researchers have studied.

• The location of Sebam is unknown. 

• The exact location of the town called Nebo is not known. However, it was likely near a mountain or ridge with the same name. This mountain stood along the steep slope (escarpment) that rises above the northern end of the Dead Sea.

• The place called Beon is almost certainly the same as “Baal-meon” in Numbers 32:38. It likely matches the ruins at Ma’in.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses assumed that Reuben and Gad wanted to stay east of the Jordan River to avoid the dangers that awaited the other tribes in Canaan (compare chapters Numbers 13:13–14).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Caleb is identified as a Kenizzite, a descendant of Esau (see Genesis 36:10–11). This suggests that Caleb was not born as an Israelite. He may have been a convert (someone who joined Israel’s faith). Even so, he became fully part of Israel’s life and worship.

Later, Caleb represented the tribe of Judah when Moses sent out the twelve spies to explore the promised land (Numbers 13:6).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Reubenites and Gadites assured Moses that they would not discourage their fellow Israelites and would support the war to its very end. There were still dangers east of the Jordan River, so they wanted to keep their livestock and families safe.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moses agreed to the terms offered by Reuben and Gad. If they helped their relatives fight the Canaanites, they would fulfill their part of the agreement. Then they could return to their settlements east of the Jordan River (Numbers 32:22). If they did not keep their promise, it would be a serious sin against God (Numbers 32:23).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Reuben and Gad kept their promise (Joshua 4:12–13; Joshua 22:1–9).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel's leaders were Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of clans. They would help enforce the commands of Moses since he would soon die (compare Joshua 22:1–2).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Gad and Reuben reaffirmed their pledge before all of Israel’s leaders.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The tribes of Gad and Reuben, along with half the tribe of Manasseh, settled east of the Jordan River (for example, Deuteronomy 3:12–13; Deuteronomy 4:43; Deuteronomy 29:7–8). These tribes lived in lands and towns captured from King Sihon the Amorite and King Og of Bashan (Numbers 32:33; see Numbers 21:21–35). 

• Half the tribe of Manasseh suddenly appears in the discussion about distributing the land. Part of Manasseh's tribe settled east of the Jordan River, while another part settled in Canaan, west of the Jordan (compare Joshua 17:1–12; Joshua 22:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The exact locations of Atroth-shophan, Jogbehah, and Beth-haran are unknown. Aroer was on the northern edge of the Arnon canyon.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Some towns may have received new names to remove connections with pagan gods. For example, Baal was the name of a well-known Canaanite god. Nebo was the name of a Babylonian god (see Isaiah 46:1). However, this passage does not give the new names of those towns.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• Three clans of Manasseh conquered part of Gilead and Bashan (compare Deuteronomy 3:13–15; Joshua 13:29–31). The exact location of Nobah is still unknown (compare Judges 8:11). 

• Havvoth-jair: Compare Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 13:30; Judges 10:4; 1 Kings 4:13; 1 Chronicles 2:21–23).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The list of travel places shows careful record-keeping. It includes many specific details. This is the only place in Numbers that says Moses wrote down part of Israel’s history (compare Exodus 24:4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• This review of the entire wilderness period includes the longest connected list of place names in the Old Testament. It begins with Israel’s departure from Egypt (Numbers 33:3; compare Exodus 12:37). It ends with their arrival in the plains of Moab, across from Jericho (Numbers 33:49; compare Numbers 22:1). 

The list names 42 stopping places along the way. These places represent more than a physical journey from one land to another. They also remind readers of Israel’s forty years of spiritual growth and testing.

Israel traveled from Rameses in Egypt (Numbers 33:3) to Abel-shittim on the plains of Moab (Numbers 33:49). During these years, the people became ready to enter the land of Canaan and receive the promises God had made to Abraham.

• This list does not give enough information to trace an exact route on a map. Many of the places cannot be identified with certainty. Some of these names do not appear anywhere else in the Hebrew Bible.

In addition, there are not enough details to locate these places precisely. The list is also selective. It does not include every place that earlier parts of the journey mention.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: marched out defiantly: See Exodus 14:8.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: executed judgment against their gods: See Exodus 6:6; Exodus 12:12. This historical review emphasizes the special events that forced Pharaoh to allow the Israelites to leave Egypt.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: For the list of Israel’s travel places between Rameses and the wilderness of Sinai, see Exodus 13:17–19:1.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Etham: See Exodus 13:20.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The exact location of Elim is not known. However, it may have been the oasis (a place with water, springs, and palm trees) at Wadi Gharandel.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The entry for Rephidim (see study note on 20:13) includes a reminder that Israel rebelled there (Exodus 7:1–7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Tradition associates the wilderness of Sinai with a mountainous region in the southern Sinai Peninsula near Jebel Musa (Arabic for “mountain of Moses”), though scholars have suggested other locations.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Kibroth-hattaavah … Hazeroth: See Numbers 11:34–12:16.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The journey between Sinai and Kadesh. Our ability to locate the named sites depends on the identification of Mount Sinai.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Most of the names of the places in this section do not appear elsewhere in the Old Testament.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Moseroth was also known as Moserah (Deuteronomy 10:6). This is where Aaron died and was buried (compare Numbers 20:22–29; Numbers 33:37–39).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Ezion-geber was located near the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba (see Deuteronomy 2:8).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel was living in Kadesh when the spies returned and gave the report of their journey through Canaan (Numbers 13:26; Numbers 27:14; “Kadesh-barnea,” Numbers 32:8).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel traveled from Kadesh to the plains of Moab.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: These details about Aaron’s death and his age show that he was about three years older than Moses (compare Numbers 20:22–29; Deuteronomy 31:1–2; Deuteronomy 34:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Many possible locations for these places are east of the Jordan River. They lie between the southern Arabah and the plains of Moab, across from Jericho.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Almon-diblathaim is probably the same place as Beth-diblathaim (Jeremiah 48:22). This place is also mentioned in the Mesha Inscription, an ancient Moabite stone monument (see study note on Numbers 21:26).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
After the Israelites arrived at the plains of Moab, across from Jericho (Numbers 22:1), they camped there. They remained in that place for the rest of the events recorded in Numbers (see Numbers 36:13; Deuteronomy 34:8). 

While they camped there, God gave Israel specific instructions on how to deal with the people of Canaan. The Lord commanded them to destroy the people groups living in Canaan and remove all traces of their religious practices (compare Exodus 23:23–33; Exodus 34:11–17; Deuteronomy 7:1–6; Deuteronomy 12:2–4; Joshua 23:4–8). 

Moses said they must destroy carved and metal idols (compare Leviticus 26:1). They were also to tear down pagan places of worship (see Deuteronomy 12:2–3).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: divide the land by lot: See Numbers 26:53–56. Chapter 34 describes the boundaries of the land of Canaan, which they would soon conquer and divide.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Israel did not follow God's instructions. So, they suffered the consequences predicted here (Numbers 33:51–53; see Judges 1:1–2:5; Judges 2:11–3:6). Israel’s enemies in the period of the judges were like "barbs … and thorns" (Numbers 33:55). Their enemies caused them military and spiritual trouble (compare 2 Corinthians 12:7).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Chapter 34 describes the borders of Canaan. This is where God commanded Israel to settle, following the guidelines in Numbers 26:52–56. Since Abraham's call, the promised land of Canaan has been central to the Old Testament story (Genesis 12:1–7). A generation of Hebrews died in the wilderness for not believing what the faithful spies reported (Numbers 13). Yet, God reaffirmed his promise of land (Numbers 33:53). 

Here, God reviews the plan and outlines the promised land's intended boundaries (compare Joshua 13–19; Ezekiel 47–48). Old Testament Israel did not fully capture this territory. It almost did during the time of the kings David and Solomon (see 2 Samuel 24:1–9). But these borders generally describe the region of Canaan as defined by Egyptian texts from 1500–1200 BC. This was when the Hebrews invaded. The region actually occupied by Israel changed from time to time.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Portions of the southern boundary of Canaan were familiar to Israel from earlier experiences in the Wilderness of Zin, located on the northwestern border of Edom (see chapters Numbers 13:13–14). This southern border curved from the southern end of the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean Sea, running east to west.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: From the southern end of the Dead Sea, the boundary ran through the Ascent of Akrabbim toward Zin (compare Numbers 13:21). The southernmost point was Kadesh-barnea (see Numbers 13:26). Hazar-addar and Azmon are unknown.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Brook of Egypt is not the Nile River. It refers to a wadi (a dry riverbed that fills with water during the rainy season). This wadi marked the border between Canaan and Egypt and flowed toward the Mediterranean Sea (see 1 Kings 8:65). I

In Old Testament times, Israel had little control over this southern coastal area.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The natural western boundary of Canaan was the Mediterranean coast ("the Great Sea," Numbers 34:6). The northern boundary started at the Mediterranean and went east to Mount Hor. This was somewhere in the Lebanon mountain range (not the place of Aaron's death, Numbers 20:22–29). 

• Lebo-hamath: Compare Numbers 13:21; 1 Kings 8:65; Amos 6:14.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Sea of Chinnereth (or Galilee): Its eastern side (literally shoulder) is the ridge that rises steeply from the eastern shore.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The natural eastern border of Canaan followed the Jordan River down to the Salt Sea (or Dead Sea). The Jordan River and the Salt Sea were part of the Great Rift Valley. They were strong barriers, but people could cross them. 

This boundary did not include the lands east of the Jordan River. Reuben, Gad, and half of the tribe of Manasseh lived there. These settlements were not part of Canaan. There were outside the first borders of the promised land.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Apportion this land by lot: Compare with Numbers 26:55–56. Two and a half tribes (Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh) settled in Transjordan (the region east of the Jordan River; compare with Numbers 32:33). So, Canaan was to be divided among the nine and a half remaining tribes.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Eleazar (the high priest) and Joshua (the political leader) were to divide the land among the remaining tribes. The 10 tribal leaders who would help them are listed in Numbers 34:19–28.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: Caleb son of Jephunneh is the only tribal leader mentioned elsewhere in Numbers (Numbers 13:6, Numbers 13:30; Numbers 14:6–38). Most of the older generation had died during the wilderness period (Numbers 26:63–65). But the two faithful spies were still leading their people.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The tribe of Levi did not receive its own land. So chapter Numbers 35:35 explains how they received 48 towns spread out among the lands of the other tribes (see Joshua 21; see also Leviticus 25:32–34; 1 Chronicles 13:2; 2 Chronicles 11:14). 

During the wilderness journey, the Levites lived in the center of the Israelite camp (compare Numbers 2:17). In the promised land, they were to live among the other tribes. Their presence was meant to influence the people for good (see Deuteronomy 33:9–10; 2 Chronicles 17:7–9; 2 Chronicles 19:8–11; 2 Chronicles 35:3). 

These towns and their pasturelands were not a separate homeland (compare Numbers 18:23; Numbers 26:62). They were only a small portion of the land of Canaan, divided among the other tribes.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Some have tried to explain the supposed contradiction between the 1,000 cubits (457 meters or 1,500 feet) and the 2,000 cubits (914 meters or 3,000 feet). One explanation is that the Hebrews thought of a town as a fixed center point. If so, the land around each town would form a square that measured 914 meters (3,000 feet) on each side. 

Another explanation is that there is a difference between the smaller pastureland mentioned in Numbers 35:4 and the larger pastureland mentioned in Numbers 35:5. 

Based on this text, some Jewish teachers later limited how far a person could walk on the Sabbath. They said a person could walk no more than 2,000 cubits (914 meters or 3,000 feet) from home.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Six of the Levites’ towns had a special purpose. They served as cities of refuge. A city of refuge was a place where a person could run for safety after accidentally killing someone.

These cities show the humanitarian (care for human life) side of Hebrew law (see also Deuteronomy 4:41–43; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; Joshua 20). 

These six towns offered protection when someone killed accidentally or unintentionally (compare Exodus 21:12–14). 

The 48 towns given to the Levites were spread throughout Israel. In the same way, the six cities of refuge were placed in different parts of the land. This made them easy to reach for anyone who needed safety (see Joshua 20:7–8). 

Before these cities were established, a person could sometimes seek safety by holding on to the altar. The altar was a place connected with worship (for example, 1 Kings 1:50–53; 1 Kings 2:28–34; compare Exodus 21:14). 

Other ancient peoples also had places of refuge. Often these places were connected to an altar (see Exodus 21:12–14; 1 Kings 2:28–34). However, only ancient Israel created entire towns as places of safety. This practice shows Israel’s special concern for justice and the protection of human life.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: a refuge from the avenger: Justice was carried out through vengeance. A designated avenger, usually a close relative of the person who died, took this role.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: the Israelites and for the foreigner or stranger among them … anyone: The same law applied equally to everyone. Israel had one standard of justice for everyone. This was unlike many societies that had different laws for citizens and noncitizens (see also Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 1 Timothy 5:21; James 2:2–4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• The Old Testament clearly distinguishes between intentional murder and accidental killing (Numbers 35:11, Numbers 35:22–23; Exodus 21:12–14; compare Numbers 15:22–31). Murder required a penalty of execution, but an accidental death did not. Murder required a penalty of execution, but an accidental death did not.

• If a person used a weapon, this showed malicious intent (a plan to harm someone).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The avenger was the victim’s closest relative. He was responsible for putting the murderer to death, carrying out the vengeance that justice required (Genesis 9:6).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Sometimes a person died, but the death was not caused by an intentional act of violence. In these cases, the person who caused the death did not plan or mean to kill anyone.

The cities of refuge were created as places of safety for people who were responsible for these accidental deaths. These cities protected them until the community could examine the case and decide what was just.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• If the person who caused the death was found not guilty of murder at a public trial before the community (compare Deuteronomy 19:11–12), that person had to remain in the city of refuge.

The avenger was not allowed to take revenge. The community had decided that the person was not guilty of murder.

• until the death of the high priest: The death of the high priest likely served as a kind of expiation (a way of removing guilt or cleansing from sin) for the blood that had been shed. Even if the person did not commit murder, the spilling of human blood was believed to pollute the land (see Numbers 35:33; compare Genesis 4:10–11).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The killer (manslayer) had to stay in a special city (called a "city of refuge") as a consequence for the death he had caused. He had to stay in a city of refuge until he or the high priest died. After the high priest's death, the manslayer could return home, and the avenger of blood could not take revenge.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: All murderers were condemned to death, but their conviction required a high standard of evidence. This included testimony from two or more witnesses (compare Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The law did not allow the payment of a ransom (money paid as compensation) to free a convicted murderer from execution. The death penalty was required for murder (compare 2 Samuel 21:2–9). Similarly, a person who caused an accidental death could not pay money to avoid staying in a city of refuge. That person had to remain there until the proper time.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
for bloodshed pollutes the land: If the person who caused a death, whether murder or accidental killing, was not treated as the law commanded, God viewed the land as polluted.

Human bloodshed required death as a response (Genesis 4:10–11; Genesis 9:6). This rule is different from cases such as Exodus 21:29–30 (see also Leviticus 18:28; Ezekiel 36:17–18; Hosea 4:2–3). 

This strong warning about murder shows the great value of human life (Exodus 20:13).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The Lord lived among the people of Israel while the Tent of Meeting (the tabernacle) was in the center of the Hebrew camp (see chapters Numbers 1:1–4). This meant that they must not defile their land. They could not ignore God’s commands. They also could not fail to carry out justice as the law required (compare Numbers 5:1–4).

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Women who inherited land might marry men from another tribe. Their land would then be lost by their ancestral tribe and transferred to their husband’s tribe. 

The "Year of Jubilee" usually allowed land to return to its original owner (Leviticus 25:8–55). But it only applied to land sold, not land gained through marriage.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content: The five daughters of Zelophehad requested and received fair property rights (Numbers 27:1–11). This passage discusses the effects of that decision.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
The Lord quickly provided the justice that the men of the tribe of Joseph asked for in their request.

Here, the tribe of Joseph refers to the tribe of Manasseh, the son of Joseph.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
These rules solved the problem. They ensured that each tribe would keep its land.

In this way, the land given to each tribe would remain stable and continue within that tribe for future generations.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
Zelophehad’s five daughters married their cousins on their father's side, as instructed. This kept their father's land within his clan. 

In ancient Hebrew society, marrying a first cousin was acceptable (compare Leviticus 18, Leviticus 20:20; see also 1 Chronicles 23:22). Other Near Eastern cultures also accepted this practice.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.content:
• commands and ordinances: These might refer to the legal instructions in the whole book (compare Leviticus 27:34). They might also refer only to the laws given on the plains of Moab (Numbers 26–36). 

• After this, only one step remained before the Israelites entered Canaan. Moses needed to remind them of their history and their covenant responsibilities. These are the main themes of the book of Deuteronomy.
